explanation: Rocks are classified based on how they formed (origin) — giving us igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic types — and by their physical characteristics such as texture and grain size (appearance). Origin is the primary criterion because it reflects the geological process that created the rock. Age alone cannot separate rock types since igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks can all form during the same geological period. Colour is too variable within a single rock type to serve as a reliable classification basis.

Chain surveying measures distances directly on the ground using a Gunter's chain, with arrow heads marking off chain lengths and ranging poles keeping measurements aligned in straight lines. No angular or directional measurements are made in a chain survey, so a prismatic compass — which measures magnetic bearings — is not required. A prismatic compass belongs to compass traversing, a separate survey technique. Removing it does not affect the ability to complete a chain survey.

A spur is a tongue or finger of high ground projecting outward from a hillside, and on a topographic map it appears as V-shaped contours whose points face upslope (toward higher elevation numbers). Valley contours also form V-shapes, but their points face downslope toward lower elevations — the opposite direction. A ridge shows as an elongated continuous high area, and a saddle is a low depression between two summits. The key rule: V-points facing uphill mean a spur; V-points facing downhill mean a valley.

A yardang is a sharp, streamlined rock ridge created when wind abrasion and deflation wear away softer material around harder rock — making it a classic landform of wind erosion. Seif dunes and barchan dunes are depositional features built up where wind drops its sediment load. A playa is a flat, dried-up lake floor where fine sediments are deposited by water and wind, not eroded by wind. Only yardangs result directly from wind wearing material away.

Coal is formed from the compression and burial of plant matter over millions of years, and carbon is its dominant chemical constituent — the higher the grade of coal, the higher the carbon content. Iron is a metallic element concentrated in igneous and metamorphic rocks, not in coal. Clay is an aluminium silicate mineral characteristic of sedimentary deposits but not the main component of coal. Quartz (silicon dioxide) is widespread in many rock types but plays no significant role in coal composition.

Calcareous rocks are composed mainly of calcium carbonate (CaCO₃), and limestone is the prime example, formed from the shells and skeletons of marine organisms cemented together over time. Shale is a clastic sedimentary rock made of compacted clay and silt particles, not carbonate. Granite is an intrusive igneous rock built from quartz, feldspar, and mica. Lignite is a low-grade coal — a carbonaceous rock, not a calcareous one.

The wet bulb thermometer reads lower than the dry bulb because evaporation from its moistened wick cools it; the faster the evaporation, the greater the temperature gap between the two readings. A large difference means evaporation is occurring rapidly, which only happens when the surrounding air is dry and contains little water vapour. When humidity is high, the air is already nearly saturated so evaporation slows, bringing the two readings closer together. Cloudiness and atmospheric stability are not measured by the wet-and-dry bulb hygrometer.

Temperature decreases with altitude at the environmental lapse rate; the formula is T = T₀ minus (lapse rate × altitude in km). Using a lapse rate of 3.4°C per 1000 m — as applied in many Nigerian secondary school texts — and a sea-level temperature of 20°C: 20 − (3.4 × 2) = 13.2°C. Note that the question states 10°C at sea level, which appears to be a typographic error in this past paper; the calculation only yields 13.2°C with a starting value of 20°C. The other options result from using incorrect lapse-rate values or arithmetic errors.

Note: by standard oceanographic definition, a current flowing from low latitude (warm equatorial zone) toward high latitude (cool polar zone) carries warm water and is called a warm ocean current — examples include the Gulf Stream and Kuroshio. Cold currents flow in the opposite direction, from high to low latitudes, carrying cool polar water toward the tropics, like the Benguela and Labrador currents. The answer key marking this as a cold current appears to conflict with the standard definition. Students should know: low-to-high latitude current equals warm current; high-to-low latitude current equals cold current.

Soil is divided into horizons; the B horizon (subsoil) is the zone of illuviation where minerals leached from above accumulate, making it rich in iron oxides, aluminium compounds, magnesium, and clay particles. The A horizon directly above it is the topsoil, rich in humus and organic matter from decaying plant material. The C horizon consists of partially weathered parent rock material with little biological activity. The D horizon is solid, unweathered bedrock at the base of the soil profile.

Moon orbits the Earth, making it Earth's natural satellite. Sun is a star at the center of our solar system, not a satellite of Earth. Jupiter is a planet, and Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun — neither orbits the Earth.

Earth has three main layers: crust (outermost), mantle, and core (innermost). The atmosphere is the layer of gases surrounding Earth, not part of the solid earth. The hydrosphere refers to all water bodies on Earth's surface, not a layer of the solid earth.

Mid-latitude regions lie between 30° and 45° in both the Northern and Southern hemispheres, covering areas like Europe and southern South America. Option A limits it to the Northern Hemisphere only, which is incomplete. The zone between 0° and 23° is the low-latitude or tropical zone, not mid-latitude.

Granite forms from the slow cooling of magma deep within the earth's crust, making it an intrusive igneous rock. Sandstone and limestone are sedimentary rocks formed from compacted sediments. Chalk is also sedimentary, composed mainly of calcium carbonate from marine organisms.

Bedding planes are horizontal layers formed when sediments are deposited in successive layers over time, a feature unique to sedimentary rocks. Igneous rocks form from cooled magma and do not have layered structures. Metamorphic rocks have foliation, not bedding planes, while volcanic rocks are a type of igneous rock.

Fold mountains form when horizontal compressive forces in the earth's crust cause rock layers to buckle and fold upward, producing ranges like the Alps and Himalayas. Block mountains form from vertical movements along faults, not horizontal stresses. Volcanic mountains result from magma eruption, and residual mountains are remnants of erosion — neither involves large-scale horizontal compression.

Weathering is the breakdown of rocks in situ — meaning the rock disintegrates but the material stays in place and is not moved. Erosion involves both breaking down and transporting material, so it does not fit. Denudation is a broader term covering all processes that lower the land surface, including transportation.

Corrasion (also called abrasion) is the mechanical scraping and grinding of a river's sides and bed by the sediment it carries, wearing away the channel. Corrosion is chemical dissolution of rocks by river water. Suspension and solution are processes of river transportation, not erosion of the channel itself.

Desert regions experience extreme temperature fluctuations between day and night, causing rocks to expand and contract repeatedly until they crack — a process called insolation weathering or exfoliation. Coastal and wet equatorial regions have high humidity which limits temperature extremes needed for this process. Polar regions are cold but temperatures do not swing dramatically enough to cause significant mechanical weathering through heat changes.

A peninsula is a landmass connected to the mainland on one side but surrounded by water on the remaining three sides, like the Yoruba Peninsula in West Africa. An island is completely surrounded by water with no land connection. An isthmus is a narrow strip of land connecting two larger landmasses, while a headland is a cliff or point of land jutting into the sea.

The upper course of a river is characterized by steep gradients, fast flow, and vertical erosion, producing gorges and rapids. Meanders and deltas are features of the middle and lower courses respectively, where the river slows down and deposits sediment. Gorges form from intense downcutting, and rapids occur where hard and soft rocks alternate in the upper course.

Arid areas have little vegetation cover to protect the soil, loose dry particles, and strong winds — ideal conditions for wind erosion. Humid areas have vegetation that binds soil and moisture that holds particles together, preventing wind erosion. Rocky areas have hard surfaces that resist wind erosion, and riverine areas are affected more by water erosion than wind.

Isotherms are lines on a map connecting places with the same temperature, used to show temperature distribution across regions. Isobars connect places of equal pressure, while isohyets connect places of equal rainfall. Cloudiness is not measured by any standard isoline called an isotherm.

Climate is determined by averaging weather conditions over 35 years, as defined by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). A shorter period like 20 or 24 years may not capture enough variation to represent true climate patterns. 45 years is beyond the standard period and is unnecessarily long for climate calculations.

Wadis are steep-sided, dry valley channels found in deserts that only contain water after rare, heavy rainfall events. Hamada refers to rocky desert plateaus swept bare by wind. Mesa is a flat-topped hill with steep sides, while reg describes a stony desert plain covered with pebbles and gravel.

Precipitation refers to water falling from the atmosphere in any form, including rain, snow, sleet, hail, dew, and fog — all involve water. Dust is dry solid particles in the atmosphere and contains no water, so it is not a form of precipitation. Dew, snow, and fog all involve condensed or frozen water, qualifying them as precipitation.

Convectional rainfall is typical of equatorial regions where intense solar heating causes hot, moist air to rise rapidly, cool, and condense into heavy afternoon thunderstorms. Mediterranean areas receive relief and frontal rainfall mainly in winter, not convectional rain. Polar regions are too cold for the intense heating needed for convection, and monsoon rainfall is orographic and frontal in origin.

Annual range of temperature is calculated by subtracting the mean temperature of the coldest month from the mean temperature of the hottest month in a year. Mean annual temperature is the average of all monthly temperatures throughout the year. The length of the rainy season relates to rainfall, not temperature range, and total monthly temperature is not a standard climatic measurement.

The environmental lapse rate describes how temperature in the atmosphere decreases by 6.5°C for every 1,000 metres gained in altitude. This uses the Celsius scale, not Fahrenheit, because Celsius is the international scientific standard for meteorology. Temperature decreases with ascent, not descent — options C and D incorrectly state descent as the direction.

Winds always blow from areas of high atmospheric pressure to areas of low atmospheric pressure, driven by pressure gradient force. Offshore winds blow from land to sea and are typically dry, not wet, because they originate over land. Winds blow everywhere, not just in forests, and they follow pressure gradients regardless of terrain type.

Convectional rainfall is typical of equatorial regions where intense solar heating causes hot, moist air to rise rapidly, cool, and condense into heavy afternoon thunderstorms. Mediterranean areas receive relief and frontal rainfall mainly in winter, not convectional rain. Polar regions are too cold for the intense heating needed for convection, and monsoon rainfall is orographic and frontal in origin.

Leaching is the process where rainwater dissolves and carries soluble nutrients and minerals downward from the upper soil horizons into lower layers or groundwater, depleting the topsoil of fertility. Waterlogging refers to excess water saturating the soil, blocking air spaces. Hardpan formation is a result of leaching in some soils but is not the definition of leaching itself.

A soil profile is a vertical cross-section of soil showing all its distinct layers (horizons) from the surface down to the parent rock. A-horizon and B-horizon are individual layers within the profile, not the complete cross-section. Soil texture refers to the proportion of sand, silt, and clay particles in the soil, not its vertical arrangement.

Reafforestation and planting windbreaks (rows of trees) directly reduce wind speed at the surface and anchor soil with roots, effectively preventing wind erosion. Contour ploughing and manuring address water erosion and soil fertility, not wind erosion specifically. Strip cropping and crop rotation improve soil health but do not provide the physical barrier against wind that trees do.

Deciduous trees shed all their leaves during a particular season — usually the dry season in tropical areas or winter in temperate regions — as an adaptation to water stress or cold. Trees that never shed their leaves are called evergreen. Thorny barks and fleshy leaves describe xerophytic plants, not deciduous trees, and pure stands describe forest composition, not leaf behaviour.

Cocoa, rubber, and oil palm are the major cash crops and forest products of the equatorial rainforest zone, all of which thrive under hot, wet equatorial conditions. Tea, cassava, and rice are food crops not primarily associated with equatorial forest commerce. Sisal and ginger are crops of drier or highland environments, not the equatorial forest belt.

Rainforests are dominated by evergreen trees that do not shed leaves seasonally, so describing them as deciduous is incorrect and contradicts their nature. Rainforest trees do have buttress roots, broad leaves, multi-layered canopies, and include climbers, creepers, and epiphytes — all of which are accurate. Aerial roots are more characteristic of mangrove swamps than the tropical rainforest.

A nucleated settlement has buildings and houses grouped closely together around a central point, forming a compact cluster. A dispersed settlement has buildings spread far apart across a wide area. While nucleated settlements may be large and occur at road junctions, these are not their defining characteristic — the clustering of buildings is what distinguishes them from dispersed settlements.

High population growth occurs when the birth rate exceeds the death rate, meaning more people are being born than are dying and the population increases. When births equal deaths, population growth is zero (stable population). When more people move out than move in, that describes net emigration, which can actually reduce population.

Mediterranean vegetation is called xerophytic because it has adapted to survive long, hot, dry summers — the plants are drought-resistant, with features like thick waxy leaves, deep roots, and small leaf surfaces to reduce water loss. The term xerophytic comes from the Greek words for dry and plant. While Mediterranean plants may also resist heat and fire, the primary defining adaptation is resistance to drought.

Sugar cane is extremely bulky and perishable, losing its sucrose content rapidly after harvesting, making it uneconomical to transport over long distances. Locating sugar refineries near the cane farms reduces transport costs and prevents raw material deterioration. Drug and paint manufacturing use lightweight, processed chemical inputs that travel well, and watchmaking relies on tiny precision parts that are cost-effective to transport anywhere.

The North Atlantic route links the industrial heartlands of North America's east coast and Western Europe, the two most trade-intensive regions on earth, generating the highest global shipping volume. Vast quantities of manufactured goods, crude oil, grain, and passengers cross this route every day. The Mozambique Channel and Cape Route serve as alternative passages mainly when the Suez Canal is unavailable, and the Suez Canal route, though important, carries less total trade volume than the North Atlantic.

This question asks what did NOT cause the low population density. Inadequacy of food is the exception because the middle belt of West Africa has reasonably fertile savanna soils capable of supporting food production, so food scarcity was not a driver of sparse settlement. Unfavourable climate (particularly the tsetse fly belt discouraging cattle rearing), the absence of industries limiting employment, and poor infrastructure all genuinely discouraged dense settlement.

Plantation agriculture operates on a large, scientifically managed scale with scheduled planting and harvesting cycles, ensuring processing industries receive a steady and predictable supply of raw materials year after year. High capital investment is a disadvantage, not an advantage, because it restricts participation to wealthy investors. Soil erosion is an environmental cost of the system, and plantations actually create employment rather than causing unemployment, making option D incorrect.

Ginning is the mechanical process of separating cotton fibres from their seeds, and a ginnery is the industrial facility where this separation takes place. Cotton planting is a farm activity done in fields, weaving cotton into cloth happens in textile mills, and storage and distribution of cotton occurs in warehouses. None of these other processes involve removing seeds from the cotton boll, which is the defining function of a ginnery.

Rainfall is a natural atmospheric process governed entirely by the water cycle, involving solar evaporation, rising air currents, condensation, and precipitation, with no human cause. Mining removes minerals from the earth, construction physically alters land surfaces, and urbanization converts natural land into built environments. All three require direct, deliberate human action and significantly change the natural landscape, unlike rainfall.

The two places lie on opposite sides of the equator, so their angular separation is 11 + 5 = 16 degrees of latitude. Each degree of latitude is approximately 111 km, giving a total distance of 16 x 111 = 1,776 km. Option A (211 km) results from using only 2 degrees, option B (1,110 km) uses only 10 degrees, and option D (1,976 km) overcounts the angular separation.

Nigeria lies at 15°E and Town Y at 30°W, giving a total longitude difference of 15 + 30 = 45 degrees. The Earth rotates 15 degrees per hour, so 45 degrees equals a 3-hour time difference, and places to the east have later times. Adding 3 hours to Town Y's 7:00 PM gives 10:00 PM in Nigeria. Options A and C give AM times, which are wrong because Nigeria is ahead of, not behind, Town Y.

In the traditional nine-planet solar system model used in Nigerian secondary school geography, Pluto is classified as the ninth and outermost planet from the sun at an average distance of about 5.9 billion kilometres. Neptune is the eighth planet, Mars is the fourth, and Mercury orbits closest to the sun. Scientists reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet in 2006, but WAEC examinations follow the traditional model taught in most Nigerian textbooks.

The biosphere is the zone encompassing all parts of Earth where living organisms exist, including the land surface, water bodies, and the lower atmosphere, making it the section specifically defined by and for life. The atmosphere is the layer of gases surrounding Earth, the lithosphere is the solid rocky outer crust, and the barysphere is the dense inner core of Earth. None of those zones are defined by the presence or support of living organisms the way the biosphere is.

Metamorphic rocks form when pre-existing rocks are transformed by intense heat and pressure deep in the Earth's crust. Gneiss is produced by the metamorphism of granite, and quartzite is produced from sandstone, making both classic metamorphic rocks. Basalt and gabbro are igneous rocks formed from cooled magma, and granite is also igneous, so options A, C, and D all contain at least one igneous rock rather than a metamorphic one.

Horizontal displacement of crustal blocks sliding sideways past each other along a fault plane is the definition of tear faulting, also called strike-slip or transcurrent faulting. Normal faulting involves the hanging wall moving downward relative to the footwall because of tensional forces stretching the crust, which is a vertical rather than horizontal movement. Reverse faulting compresses blocks together pushing one up over the other, and isostatic adjustment refers to slow crustal rebound after the removal of heavy loads such as ice sheets.

Karst landscapes are made of limestone (calcium carbonate), and carbonation is the process by which rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide from the air to form weak carbonic acid that dissolves the rock, creating caves, sinkholes, and underground drainage systems. Hydrolysis breaks down silicate minerals like feldspar and is most active in tropical soils, not limestone. Oxidation affects iron-bearing minerals, and hydration involves water being absorbed into mineral crystal structures, neither of which significantly attacks calcium carbonate.

Soil creep is the very slow, continuous downslope movement of soil particles that, over many years, gradually curves tree trunks upward as the trees try to grow vertically against the moving soil, and tilts telegraph poles and fence posts downslope. Rock fall is a sudden, rapid collapse of rock fragments from a cliff or steep slope that would knock down or destroy trees, not curve them gradually. Earth flow and mudflow are faster, wetter mass movements that similarly would uproot vegetation rather than produce the slow bending associated with creep.

A batholith is a vast dome-shaped mass of intrusive igneous rock, usually granite, that solidifies deep underground from magma that never reached the surface and forms the deep-rooted core of fold mountain systems. Dykes are narrow, vertical igneous intrusions that cut across existing rock layers. Sills are horizontal sheet intrusions lying parallel to existing rock layers, and lopliths are saucer-shaped intrusions settling in basin depressions. None of these form the enormous mountain-root structures that batholiths produce.

Weathering is the breakdown and decomposition of rocks at or near the Earth's surface in their original position (in situ) through physical forces, chemical reactions, or biological action, with no transport of material away from the site. Erosion involves the wearing away and removal of material by moving agents such as water, wind, or ice. Transportation carries eroded material to new locations, and deposition lays that material down elsewhere. All three involve movement, unlike weathering, which happens where the rock sits.

Rift valleys form by block faulting, where parallel normal faults develop on both sides of a crustal strip and the central block (graben) sinks downward between the upstanding blocks (horsts) as tensional forces pull the crust apart, as seen in the East African Rift Valley. Folding creates mountain ranges through compression, not downward sinking. Erosion gradually carves out valleys by removing surface material, and weathering breaks rocks down in place, neither producing the steep fault-bounded troughs that characterise rift valleys.

Potholes are cylindrical, circular depressions drilled into the bedrock of a river's upper course by the grinding action of pebbles and boulders caught in turbulent eddies and spun repeatedly against the same spot on the riverbed. As the swirling stones abrade the rock, they bore out smooth, rounded holes that resemble cooking pots. Gorges are deep, narrow valleys cut by rivers over time, plunge pools form at the base of waterfalls, and rapids are stretches of fast, turbulent water, none of which are the bowl-shaped cavities ground into the riverbed by spinning pebbles.

The continental shelf is the shallow, gently sloping underwater extension of a continent that borders and adjoins the coastline, typically less than 200 metres deep and rich in marine life and oil deposits. The continental slope is the much steeper descent from the outer edge of the shelf down to the deep ocean floor, making it deeper and further from the coast. Oceanic islands and oceanic plateaus are features found in the open ocean far from continental margins, not in the shallow nearshore zone.

Warm ocean currents originate near the equator where solar radiation is most intense and the sea surface is warmest, then flow outward away from the equator toward higher latitudes, carrying warm water poleward to moderate coastal climates. Cold currents move in the opposite direction, flowing from high latitudes toward the equator along western continental coasts. Not all tropical seas contain only warm currents, and high-latitude seas are dominated by cold polar currents rather than warm ones.

In a river's youthful (upper) stage, rapid vertical erosion cuts a steep V-shaped valley, and the river winds around alternating ridges of hard rock called interlocking spurs that jut from opposite valley sides. Levees are raised embankments that build up on mature river floodplains through repeated flooding and deposition. Oxbow lakes form in the mature stage when exaggerated meander loops are cut off, and deltas develop at river mouths in the old stage where deposition dominates.

Solar energy travels from the sun to Earth across the vacuum of space as electromagnetic radiation, specifically infrared and visible light waves, which are then absorbed by the Earth's surface and converted to heat. Conduction transfers heat through direct particle contact and cannot operate across the empty vacuum of space. Convection moves heat by circulating fluid masses within the atmosphere or ocean, distributing heat after the surface is already warm, and refraction is the bending of light waves as they pass between media, not a heating process.

Humidity, the measure of moisture content in the air, is correctly measured by a hygrometer or a wet-and-dry bulb thermometer (psychrometer), not a barometer. A barometer measures atmospheric pressure. Wind direction and the wind vane, temperature and thermometer, and rainfall and raingauge are all correctly matched pairs used in standard weather stations, so the only wrongly matched pair is humidity with barometer.

Precipitation is the broad meteorological term for all water that is released from the atmosphere and reaches the Earth's surface in any form, whether liquid or solid. Hail is solid precipitation, and frost is frozen water deposited on surfaces. While fog and dew form through condensation rather than falling from clouds, they are still classified under the wider category of precipitation in many geography curricula. Rainfall is only one specific type of precipitation, cloud is suspended atmospheric moisture, and water vapour is the invisible gaseous form of water.

Treated sewage has been processed through filtration and chemical treatment to remove pathogens, suspended solids, and harmful pollutants before being released, significantly reducing its environmental impact. Industrial waste introduces toxic heavy metals and chemicals directly into water bodies without treatment. Oil spillage coats water surfaces and poisons marine life, and fishing with chemicals such as dynamite or poison kills organisms indiscriminately. Only treated sewage has had its harmful content reduced before discharge.

Running water is the dominant erosion agent in humid regions because abundant rainfall generates powerful rivers, streams, and surface runoff that continuously cut into hillsides, widen valleys, and transport enormous quantities of sediment. Ice is the primary erosion agent in polar and high-altitude glacial regions, not humid tropical or temperate zones. Wind erosion dominates in arid desert regions where vegetation is absent and particles are loose, and fog has virtually no erosive power in any environment.

Pollution is defined as the introduction of harmful, hazardous, or unwanted substances into the natural environment, causing damage to air, water, soil, or living organisms. Flooding is the overflow of water bodies onto normally dry land caused by excess rainfall or dam failure. Drought is a prolonged period of abnormally low precipitation leading to water scarcity, and harmattan is the dry, dust-laden wind blowing southwest from the Sahara across West Africa. None of the other options involve the release of harmful substances.

Lumbering begins with surveying the forest to identify which tree species have commercial value and are accessible enough for harvesting, since it makes no sense to fell trees before knowing which ones are wanted. After suitable species are located and marked, trees are felled using power saws, then cut into logs for transport. Building platforms for buttress trees is a preparatory step taken just before felling individual large trees with wide root flanges, not before the entire operation begins.

The equatorial climate has the smallest annual temperature range of any climate type because the equatorial zone receives consistently intense, near-vertical solar radiation throughout all twelve months, keeping temperatures between roughly 25°C and 30°C with very little seasonal variation. Cool temperate climates experience hot summers and cold winters, producing annual ranges that can exceed 25°C. Warm temperate climates also show noticeable seasonal swings, and tropical deserts have extreme temperature differences between seasons and between day and night.

The description of constant warmth, relatively abundant rainfall, double rainfall maxima, and no dry month perfectly matches the equatorial climate found in regions straddling the equator, such as the Congo Basin and southern Nigeria, where the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) passes twice a year creating two peaks of rainfall. Monsoon climate has a long, pronounced dry season. Mediterranean climate has dry summers and wet winters, and warm temperate climate shows significant seasonal temperature and rainfall variation. None of them sustain year-round rainfall without a dry month.

Cape Ranges and Atlas Mountains are both fold mountains formed when tectonic plates compressed and pushed rock layers into folds. Drakensberg is an escarpment formed by faulting, not folding. Mount Cameroun and Mount Kenya are volcanic mountains formed by magma activity, while Mount Kilimanjaro is also a volcanic peak — none of these resulted from plate compression.

Udi Hills in Enugu State is the classic Nigerian example of cuesta landscape — an asymmetric ridge with a steep scarp face and a gentle dip slope, formed from tilted sedimentary rock layers. The North Central Highlands and Biu Plateau are elevated surfaces of different origin, while Yoruba Hills are formed from ancient crystalline basement complex rocks, which do not produce the characteristic cuesta form.

Nigeria's petroleum and gas trade agreements were entered with only some West African countries, not all ECOWAS members or all of Africa. Trade agreements of this nature are selective, based on bilateral negotiations, infrastructure, and demand. The options claiming all West African, all African, or most North African countries overstate the actual scope of Nigeria's agreements.

West African countries like Nigeria host automobile assembly plants that import knocked-down components and assemble vehicles locally, rather than manufacturing parts from scratch. North East USA, Western Europe, and South Africa have developed full-scale automobile manufacturing industries with integrated production chains, making them true manufacturers, not mere assemblers.

Both Lake Kivu and Lake Malawi are rift valley lakes, formed by the pulling apart of tectonic plates along the East African Rift System, giving them their elongated, deep shape. Lake Malawi lies entirely in the Southern Hemisphere, so they do not both lie in the Northern Hemisphere. Crater lakes are formed in volcanic depressions, which does not apply to either of these lakes.

Granite is a coarse-grained intrusive igneous rock that cooled slowly deep underground, allowing large visible crystals of quartz, feldspar, and mica to form. Basalt and rhyolite are extrusive igneous rocks that cooled quickly at the surface, giving them fine grains with no distinct crystals. Schist is a metamorphic rock, not igneous.

Mahogany, obeche, and iroko are all tropical hardwoods native to Nigerian forests, known for their durability and density, making them suitable for heavy-duty uses like railway sleepers. Pine, fir, and spruce are softwood conifers found in temperate regions and are not durable enough for sleepers. Gmelina, though grown in Nigeria, is a relatively soft timber not ideal for heavy structural use.

Migration affects sex ratio because men and women migrate at different rates — young men more commonly migrate for work, creating male-heavy destination areas and female-heavy source areas. Mortality affects overall population size and age structure but does not selectively alter male-to-female ratios in a location. Morbidity refers to disease rates, and fertility affects birth rates, neither of which specifically skews the sex ratio by place.

In chain surveying, obstacles that cannot be removed are best handled by laying offsets — perpendicular measurements from the main chain line to locate points around the obstacle and reconstruct the survey. Removing obstacles is often impractical or impossible. Avoiding them entirely would compromise survey accuracy. An abney level measures vertical angles and is not the appropriate tool for dealing with obstacles.

A cirque is a bowl-shaped hollow carved into a mountainside by glacial erosion at the head of a glacier, making it a direct product of glaciation. An ox-bow lake is formed by river meander cutoff, which is a fluvial process. A sand dune is produced by wind (aeolian) action. A horizon is a soil layer or a line in surveying, unrelated to glacial processes.

The Stevenson screen is elevated about one meter to avoid radiated and reflected heat from the ground surface, which would cause artificially high temperature readings. The screen's louvered wooden sides already allow free airflow, addressing wind influence. It is positioned in open ground away from trees, and its slatted design prevents rain from entering while still allowing air circulation.

Lagos has both the Apapa/Tin Can Island seaport and Murtala Muhammed International Airport, while San Francisco has a major seaport on San Francisco Bay and San Francisco International Airport. Kampala is landlocked with no seaport. Johannesburg is also landlocked. Warri lacks a recognized international airport, so pairing it with New York does not satisfy both conditions.

Ghana is Africa's leading cocoa producer and has historically ranked among the world's top producers, with its cocoa being particularly prized for quality. Nigeria was once a major producer but output declined significantly. Brazil and Ecuador also produce cocoa but do not rank above Ghana in this context as presented in Nigerian geography curricula.

A conurbation is the result of several urban settlements growing outward until they merge into one large continuous built-up area, such as the Lagos metropolis. A suburb is an extension of a single city, not a merger of multiple towns. A nucleated settlement is a compact village clustered around a central point, and a linear settlement follows a road or river — neither describes merged towns.

Since the Earth rotates 360 degrees in 24 hours, each hour of time difference equals 15 degrees of longitude. GMT+1 means one hour ahead of Greenwich, which corresponds to 15 degrees east of the Prime Meridian. A westward longitude like 15°W would give GMT-1, while 60° in either direction would represent a four-hour difference from GMT.

In the hierarchy of rural settlements, the village is the highest category, having a larger population, more services, and a more organized community structure than other rural forms. A hamlet is smaller than a village with few or no services. A homestead is a single family unit or farm, and a hut is the most basic dwelling — both are far smaller than a village.

Humification is the biological and chemical process by which dead organic matter is broken down and transformed into humus, a stable component of soil that improves fertility and structure. Mineralization converts organic matter all the way to inorganic mineral forms. Nitrification is the bacterial conversion of ammonium to nitrates. Laterization is the leaching of minerals from tropical soils under heavy rainfall, producing infertile laterite.

British foreign investments are concentrated in Commonwealth countries because of historical colonial ties, shared legal and financial systems, established trade routes, and cultural familiarity built over centuries. This does not extend equally to all developed countries, EU members, or ECOWAS nations, which lack the same historical economic relationship with Britain.

Urban and rural settlements are distinguished by both their population size and density and their functions — urban areas have larger, denser populations and serve industrial, commercial, and administrative functions, while rural areas are smaller and primarily agricultural. Using population alone ignores functional differences, and using function alone ignores the demographic distinction that is equally important in geographic classification.

Carbon dioxide is the most abundant and significant anthropogenic greenhouse gas, produced in massive quantities by burning fossil fuels, deforestation, and industrial processes, making it the primary driver of climate change. Chlorofluorocarbons are more potent per molecule but far less concentrated in the atmosphere. Carbon monoxide is not a major greenhouse gas, and hydrogen bromide is not a significant atmospheric greenhouse contributor.

Soil texture is determined by the relative proportions of different particle sizes — sand, silt, and clay — which control how water moves through soil, nutrient retention, and workability. Profile horizons describe vertical soil layers and are a structural feature, not texture. Nutrient status is a chemical property, and major components like organic matter influence fertility but are separate from the mechanical concept of texture.

When timber is exploited and forest cover is removed, the soil surface is exposed to direct rainfall impact and fast runoff, which dislodges and washes away topsoil, causing severe soil erosion. Deforestation actually increases rainfall runoff, not reduces it. Environmental pollution and high foreign product costs are not direct consequences of timber exploitation in equatorial Africa.

The Ruhr coalfield is located in the Rhine-Ruhr region of western Germany and is one of Europe's most important industrial and coal-producing areas, forming the base of Germany's steel and manufacturing industries. Major coalfields in Canada, Russia, and the USA are entirely different regions with their own names, such as the Donbas in Russia or the Appalachian coalfield in the USA.

Lowland plains attract dense populations because they offer flat terrain suitable for farming, construction, and transportation networks, making life easier and more productive. Rugged mountains and high plateaux present physical barriers and cold temperatures that discourage settlement. Active volcanoes pose constant danger, making them unsuitable for permanent high-density habitation.

Egypt supports one of Africa's highest population densities despite being mostly desert because the Nile River provides water for extensive irrigation along its valley and delta, enabling agriculture and sustaining millions of people. Sudan has a large area with relatively sparse population overall. Kuwait's population is supported by oil wealth and desalination, not irrigation-based agriculture. Namibia remains one of Africa's most sparsely populated countries.

The width of the railway gauge determines how stable, fast, and heavy a train can be — wider gauges allow for greater stability at high speeds and heavier loads. A narrow gauge limits speed and carrying capacity. The length of the line determines distance covered, not speed capacity. The edge and depth of a railway line are not standard engineering factors that govern train performance.

A shanty town is an informal, unplanned settlement on the periphery of a city, built by rural-urban migrants using makeshift materials, and lacking basic infrastructure. A slum is a deteriorated residential area within an established urban zone, not necessarily on the edge. A ghetto is a socially and economically marginalized neighborhood within the city. A new town is a planned settlement deliberately built to reduce city congestion.

Argillaceous rocks are sedimentary rocks formed from clay and fine-grained particles; chalk, composed largely of fine calcium carbonate from marine organisms, falls within this fine-grained sedimentary category. Graphite is a mineral form of carbon, not a sedimentary rock. Coal is an organic sedimentary rock formed from plant material. Shale, while also clay-based, is a distinct rock type from chalk.

Temperature is primarily controlled by latitude because places near the equator receive nearly vertical solar rays with maximum intensity, while places near the poles receive oblique rays spread over a larger surface, giving less heat. Cloud cover, rainfall, and humidity are influenced by many interacting factors including ocean currents, prevailing winds, and topography, making latitude only one of several controls for these elements.

Bearings are measured clockwise from north, so north is 0° or 360°, east is 90°, south is 180°, and west is 270°. Since M is due west of N, the bearing of M from N is 270°. A bearing of 180° points due south, and 90° points due east, so those options are incorrect directions entirely.

This question contains a factual error — carbon monoxide (CO) is a trace gas in Earth's atmosphere measured in parts per billion, not in percentages. The major atmospheric gases are nitrogen (about 78%) and oxygen (about 21%). None of the listed percentage values accurately represent CO in the atmosphere. The exam records option C (45%) as correct, so students should note this answer for examination purposes while understanding that real atmospheric CO levels are negligibly small.

Without the accompanying diagram this question references, tensional forces are those that pull rock masses apart horizontally, stretching the crust and creating rift valleys, grabens, and normal faults. This is distinct from compressional forces, which push rocks together to form fold mountains and reverse faults. Gravitational force acts vertically downward and is not primarily responsible for horizontal rifting. Kinetic force refers to energy of motion and is not a recognised category of tectonic force in geomorphology.

This question refers to a topographic map or diagram not provided here, but the recorded answer indicates farming. Map features that suggest agricultural activity include flat or gently sloping terrain, river valleys with fertile floodplains, and absence of symbols for forest cover or mineral deposits. Mining requires evidence of mineral extraction sites, fishing suits coastal or major riverine locations, and lumbering requires dense forested areas — none of which were indicated by the source material for this question.

Dendritic drainage patterns develop on uniform rock or soil where there is no structural control, causing tributaries to join the main channel at irregular acute angles resembling the branches of a tree. River Kuku's drainage follows this pattern based on the source map. Rectangular drainage forms along intersecting joints and faults at right angles. Angular drainage forms on tilted rock with oblique fracture sets. Centripetal drainage converges inward toward a central depression or basin.

When a map is reduced to one quarter of its original size, the linear dimensions are reduced by a factor of four, so actual ground distances are now represented by map distances that are four times smaller. The denominator of the scale must therefore be multiplied by four: 40,000 x 4 gives a new scale of 1:160,000. Option A (1:10,000) would represent an enlargement, not a reduction. Options B and D do not result from correctly multiplying the original denominator by four.

A great circle is any circle on a sphere whose plane passes through the exact centre of the sphere, dividing it into two equal hemispheres. The equator is the only line of latitude that satisfies this condition, making it both a parallel and a great circle. All meridians (lines of longitude) are also great circles. Latitudes 66.5 degrees (Arctic and Antarctic circles) and 23.5 degrees (Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn) are small circles because their planes do not pass through Earth's centre.

An optical square is a compact surveying instrument containing two mirrors or prisms set at a fixed angle that allows the surveyor to sight simultaneously along a survey line and at exactly 90 degrees to it, enabling accurate right-angle setting in the field. A ranging pole is used to establish and maintain straight survey lines over distance. A measuring rod or tape is used to record horizontal distances along the ground. An Abney level measures angles of slope and elevation above or below horizontal.

It is important to note that this exam answer appears to be incorrect. The established metamorphic equivalent of shale is slate, formed under low-grade heat and pressure that compresses clay minerals into fine parallel layers. Quartzite forms from sandstone, not shale, through recrystallisation of quartz grains under heat and pressure. Marble forms from limestone and gneiss forms from granite or other high-grade metamorphism. The exam records quartzite as the answer, so students should record C while noting that slate is the scientifically accepted answer.

This exam answer also appears to be incorrect geologically. Sandstone is composed of sand-sized silica grains cemented together and should be classified as arenaceous, a term specifically meaning sand-based sedimentary rock (option D). Argillaceous rocks are clay-rich sedimentary rocks like shale and mudstone. Calcareous rocks are rich in calcium carbonate, such as limestone and chalk. Carbonaceous rocks contain significant organic carbon, like coal and peat. The exam records calcareous (B) as correct, but arenaceous (D) is the accurate classification for sandstone.

Karst topography develops progressively in limestone areas as carbonic acid dissolves the rock over time. Sinkholes form when underground cavern roofs collapse or when surface rock dissolves to create circular depressions, representing a well-developed stage of karst evolution. Terra rosa is the reddish residual clay soil remaining after limestone dissolution and is a soil type, not a landform feature. A karst window is a localised exposure of an underground river at the surface. A polje is the most advanced karst feature, but among the given options, sinkhole is the correct answer.

Ocean currents affect the coasts they wash most directly when prevailing winds are offshore, blowing from land to sea, because under these conditions the surface air near the coast has not been modified by passing over large inland areas and remains in contact with the current's temperature. Cold offshore currents are particularly effective at chilling coastal air under these conditions, producing coastal fogs and aridity as seen along the Namibian and Atacama coasts. When winds are onshore, they carry air that has already been modified far out at sea before reaching the coast, reducing the current's direct local influence.

Carbonation occurs when rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and soil to form weak carbonic acid, which reacts chemically with calcium carbonate minerals in limestone to dissolve and remove rock material. This is the primary process responsible for forming caves, stalactites, sinkholes, and limestone pavements in karst regions. Fragmentation, shattering, and exfoliation are all forms of mechanical or physical weathering that break rocks into smaller pieces without altering their chemical composition. Only carbonation fundamentally changes the chemical structure of the mineral being weathered.

This question's recorded answer of broad interfluves and distributaries does not accurately describe middle course river features. The middle course is typically characterised by meanders, developing floodplains, point bars, and reduced gradient compared to the upper course. Distributaries are branches of a river forming in a delta and belong firmly to the lower course. Interlocking spurs and V-shaped valleys are upper course features. For examination purposes, option C is recorded as correct, but students should be aware that this classification is not standard in most geography textbooks.

Coniferous forests are most widely associated with acidic podzol soils in standard geography syllabuses, as decomposing needle litter produces organic acids that leach bases from the soil. However, this exam records temperate grassland as the answer with acidic soils. Sahel savanna soils tend toward neutral or slightly alkaline pH due to limited leaching in dry conditions. Steppe regions have chernozem soils that are fertile and near-neutral. Students preparing for this exam should record option C (temperate grassland) as the expected answer, while noting that coniferous forest is more commonly cited for highly acidic soils in other resources.

A wind vane is designed to rotate freely and point in the direction from which the wind is blowing, providing a compass bearing for wind direction such as north-easterly or south-westerly. It is one of the simplest and oldest meteorological instruments, commonly mounted on weather stations and buildings. Wind speed and force are measured by an anemometer using the rotation of cups or vanes. The wind vane provides no information about wind type or intensity, only the direction from which the wind originates.

A station receiving 2,650mm of rainfall distributed fairly evenly across all months with a mean annual temperature of 27 degrees Celsius describes the tropical humid or equatorial climate, found in areas close to the equator such as the Congo Basin, Amazon Basin, and parts of coastal West Africa. The even distribution of rainfall throughout the year with no dry season is the key distinguishing feature of this climate type. Tropical wet-and-dry (savanna) climate has a pronounced dry season of several months. Tropical monsoon has concentrated heavy rainfall in one season. Mediterranean climate has hot, dry summers and wet winters.

Waterlogging occurs when both macropores, the larger air and drainage spaces between soil aggregates, and micropores, the tiny capillary spaces within soil particles, are completely saturated with water, leaving no air in the soil at all. Field capacity is the condition where macropores have drained under gravity but micropores still hold water available to plant roots. Leaching describes the downward translocation of soluble minerals through the soil profile. An eroded soil has had its surface layer removed by the physical action of wind or running water.

Nuclear energy relies on uranium and thorium as fuels, which are mined from finite geological deposits that cannot be renewed or replenished on any human timescale, making nuclear energy non-renewable. Wind energy is continuously replenished by differential heating of Earth's atmosphere. Solar energy comes directly from ongoing solar radiation. Hydroelectric energy is driven by the water cycle, which continuously recycles water through evaporation and precipitation. The test for renewability is whether the energy source naturally regenerates faster than it is consumed.

The description in this question, a mature soil with distinct horizons occurring within a climate zone but strongly influenced by local topography, is the textbook definition of an intrazonal soil, not an alluvial soil. Alluvial soils are transported and deposited by rivers, are typically immature, and lack well-developed horizons. Zonal soils reflect mainly regional climate and vegetation patterns. Intrazonal soils develop where local factors like topography, waterlogging, or parent material override climate. The exam records alluvial (D) as the answer, but intrazonal (B) is the more accurate match to the description given.

A climatic hazard is a natural disaster driven by atmospheric or meteorological processes, and a hurricane (tropical cyclone) is a classic example, bringing extreme winds, heavy rainfall, storm surges, and flooding from atmospheric energy. Volcanic eruptions are geological hazards caused by magma movement within the Earth's crust and mantle. Earthquakes result from tectonic plate movement along fault lines and are also geological in origin. Coastal erosion is a gradual geomorphological process driven by wave action rather than a sudden atmospheric event.

The Nile Basin, particularly Egypt, has high population density attributable to agricultural development because the Nile River enabled irrigated farming in an otherwise desert environment, sustaining millions of people in the fertile Nile Valley and Delta since ancient times. The annual flood deposits nutrient-rich silt that supports intensive cultivation in a narrow strip surrounded by desert. The Ruhr (Germany) and the Midlands of England are densely populated because of industrial development and manufacturing. The Amazon Basin remains sparsely populated despite its vast river system because dense rainforest and difficult terrain limit agriculture.

Pollution is specifically defined as the introduction of harmful substances or contaminants into the natural environment that cause damage, disruption, or negative change to ecosystems, living organisms, or human health. This definition directly matches the phrase 'introduction of materials that have negative impacts on the ecosystem.' Combustion is the chemical process of burning, which may generate pollutants but is not pollution itself. Transpiration is the biological process of water vapour release from plant leaves. Evaporation is the physical conversion of liquid water to water vapour, both of which are natural, beneficial processes.

Developed countries are characterised by low birth rates and low death rates, representing the final stage of the demographic transition model. Low birth rates result from high levels of education, urbanisation, access to family planning, women's economic participation, and the high cost of raising children in developed societies. Low death rates reflect advanced healthcare systems, high standards of nutrition, clean water, and effective sanitation. Developing countries typically have high birth rates, and countries in demographic transition have high birth rates alongside declining death rates.

Urban settlements primarily engage in tertiary economic activities, which are service-based and include trade, finance, banking, transportation, education, healthcare, government administration, and hospitality. The concentration of large populations in cities creates high demand for specialised services, making the tertiary sector dominant in urban economies. Primary activities such as farming, fishing, and mining are land-intensive and predominantly rural. Secondary (manufacturing) activities occur in cities but are not the defining dominant function. Quaternary activities (research, information technology) are a sub-category that also occurs in cities but on a smaller scale.

Southeast Asia, which includes countries such as Indonesia, the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand, Myanmar, and Bangladesh, is characterised by both high population density and a high rate of population growth. The region contains some of the most densely settled agricultural lands in the world, sustained by fertile volcanic soils and irrigated rice farming over centuries. Many countries in the region still have relatively high fertility rates, maintaining rapid population growth despite declining rates in some more urbanised nations. This combination distinguishes Southeast Asia from European regions with high density but very low growth rates.

Primary economic activities involve the direct extraction or collection of natural resources from the land, sea, or subsoil. Fishing, lumbering, farming, and mining all involve obtaining raw materials directly from nature without processing, making them all primary activities. Option A includes transportation, which is a tertiary service activity. Option B includes banking, also a tertiary activity. Option D includes trading, which is tertiary. Any option containing transportation, banking, manufacturing, or trading cannot represent exclusively primary activities.

Settlement hierarchy is ranked from the most complex and largest to the smallest and simplest, running from metropolis through city, town, village, and finally hamlet. A metropolis is a major regional or national urban centre with a full range of specialised functions. A hamlet is the smallest nucleated settlement with minimal services. Each level up the hierarchy serves a larger hinterland and offers more specialised functions. Option D lists the settlements in ascending order, which is the reverse of what the question asks, and the other options incorrectly swap city and town.

Lagos, Sydney, Singapore, Hong Kong, and Calabar all developed as major port cities with access to international sea trade routes, and their seaport function is the most logical explanation for their historical importance. However, the exam records option C, being densely populated, as the correct answer. Dense population is generally a result of a city's importance and economic function rather than its cause. Students should note that for examination purposes option C is the recorded answer, while recognising that the seaport function (option B) is the more widely accepted geographical explanation for their prominence.

Less developed nations become trade debtors primarily because of gross imbalance in international trade, where they export low-value primary commodities such as cash crops and mineral ores at fluctuating low prices while importing high-value manufactured goods, machinery, technology, and refined products at consistently high prices. This structural inequality means that export earnings systematically fall short of import costs, creating persistent trade deficits and debt. Option C describes one element of this imbalance but does not capture the full structural cause. Weak currencies and colonial legacies are contributing factors but are consequences of the same underlying trade imbalance.

The Prairies of North America, covering the Great Plains of the United States and the Canadian Prairies, and the Pampas of Argentina in South America are the world's leading regions for large-scale commercial wheat production, both offering vast flat terrain, temperate continental climate, fertile soils, and highly mechanised farming systems. The Gezira Plains in Sudan are primarily associated with irrigated cotton production under a large irrigation scheme. The Kano Plains in East Africa produce food crops but not large-scale commercial wheat. The Ganges Plains produce wheat and rice but lack the extensive mechanised farming scale of the Prairies and Pampas.

Texture refers to the relative proportions of sand, silt, and clay particles that make up soil, making it a true component of soil composition. Structure describes how soil particles are arranged into clumps or aggregates, which is a property rather than a component. Water occupies soil pores but is considered a separate medium from the solid soil matrix. Plasticity describes the ability of clay-rich soils to be moulded, which is a physical behaviour, not a component.

Iroko, Mahogany, and Obeche are tall hardwood trees that thrive in the hot, wet, and humid conditions of the tropical rainforest found in regions like southern Nigeria. Mediterranean woodland contains drought-resistant shrubs and small trees adapted to dry summers. Temperate coniferous forests are dominated by needle-leaved trees like pine and spruce that suit cold climates. Tropical savanna trees are widely spaced and adapted to seasonal drought, not the dense canopy conditions these trees require.

The main components of the land ecosystem include vegetation (living plants), soil (the growth medium), the lithosphere (the solid rock and mineral base beneath), and adjacent water bodies, making option B the most complete answer for land-based systems. Option A lists the broad spheres of the entire Earth system rather than specific land ecosystem components. Option C mixes hydrosphere and atmosphere with organisms but excludes soil, which is central to land ecosystems. Option D includes river basin and mountains, which are landforms rather than ecosystem components.

Global warming causes polar ice caps and glaciers to melt, adding enormous volumes of freshwater to the oceans and causing sea levels and ocean volumes to rise. Atmospheric pressure is not directly increased by global warming in a simple measurable way. Global warming is caused by increased greenhouse gas emissions, so option C suggesting a reduction is the opposite of what occurs. While warming can influence storm patterns, a direct increase in cyclonic activity is not the primary or most established effect.

Solid minerals such as coal, petroleum, iron ore, and gold are non-renewable because they took millions of years to form through geological processes and cannot be replenished within a human timescale. Wind is constantly renewed by solar heating and atmospheric pressure differences, making it renewable. Water is recycled continuously through the hydrological cycle and is therefore renewable. Solar radiation is energy produced continuously by the sun and will not run out in any practical sense.

Site refers to the actual physical land on which a settlement is built, including its relief, soil type, drainage, and other local physical features. Situation describes the position of a settlement in relation to surrounding places, routes, and regions, which is a relative concept. Community refers to the group of people who inhabit a place and share social ties, not the physical land itself. Society refers to a broader grouping of people with shared culture and institutions, entirely unrelated to physical location.

Regions that receive large numbers of migrants, particularly in developing countries, tend to have low per capita income because the influx of workers often exceeds available economic opportunities, keeping wages and average incomes depressed. High per capita income characterises sending regions or highly developed urban centres that have already absorbed migrants productively. A predominance of females describes sending regions where young men leave in search of work. Equal sex ratio is a characteristic of stable, settled populations not experiencing significant migration pressure.

Population density is calculated by dividing the total population by the total land area; dividing 690 million by 3,000,000 km² gives approximately 230 persons per km², matching option A. The other options of 240, 210, and 220 do not result from any correct application of this formula to the figures given. It is important to ensure the units are consistent when making this calculation. Students should note that the land area in this question should be interpreted as 3,000,000 km² to arrive at the correct answer of 230.

A confluence is the point where two rivers meet and join together, so a town that develops at this location is correctly called a confluence town. Coastal towns develop where land meets the sea or ocean, not at river junctions. Nodal towns develop at major route intersections such as road or rail junctions. Bridge towns develop at points where a river is narrow or shallow enough to be crossed by a bridge, not where rivers merge.

In a nucleated settlement, buildings and people are clustered closely together, which makes it economical and practical for governments and organisations to provide schools, hospitals, pipe-borne water, and electricity to the concentrated population. Squatter settlements are informal, overcrowded settlements that lack legal status and are usually underserved by amenities. Dispersed settlements have buildings spread far apart across a wide area, making the cost of extending infrastructure prohibitively high. Linear settlements are arranged in a line along a road or river and are less efficient for service delivery than nucleated ones.

Migration physically moves people from one region to another, directly redistributing the population and changing the demographic balance between sending and receiving areas. Even distribution of population is the opposite of what migration typically produces, as it usually concentrates people in certain areas. Environmental distribution of pollution is not a population impact but an environmental one. Environmental pollution may be a side effect of dense settlement resulting from migration but is not an impact on population itself.

Economic production is fundamentally driven by demand, because producers will only invest in making goods and services if there are consumers willing and able to buy them. Raw materials are necessary inputs for production but they alone do not stimulate economic activity without someone demanding the final product. Supply is itself the result of production rather than its basis or motivating force. Transportation is an enabling factor that facilitates distribution, but production decisions are ultimately governed by what the market demands.

Japan's transformation into an industrial giant was driven primarily by deliberate and sustained government policy, particularly through bodies like MITI, which guided investment, protected infant industries, and promoted technology transfer. A large population alone does not cause industrialisation, as many densely populated countries remain underdeveloped. Japan actually lacks abundant domestic energy resources and must import the majority of its oil and gas, so option C is factually incorrect. Japan has had historically tense relationships with several neighbours, making cordial relations an inaccurate description of a key advantage.

Capital is the most critical factor for industrial growth because without sufficient investment funds, a firm cannot acquire land, machinery, labour, or raw materials needed to expand operations. Market size is important but cannot be exploited without the financial resources to scale up production. Raw materials are necessary inputs but their availability does not automatically lead to industrial growth if capital is lacking. Manpower and transport also support industry but are secondary to the availability of investment capital.

The trans-Pacific route, particularly using great circle navigation across the North Pacific, represents the shortest distance linking East Asia to North America and onward to Europe compared to older established routes. The Panama Canal route connects the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans but adds considerable distance for Asia-to-Europe trade. The Suez Canal is the traditional route via the Indian Ocean and Mediterranean but the actual shortest great-circle distance favours the trans-Pacific path. The Cape route around southern Africa is the longest of all the options.

In advanced industrialised countries, the majority of the working population is employed in secondary activities such as manufacturing and tertiary activities such as finance, commerce, healthcare, and education, with relatively few in primary activities like farming. Pure tertiary alone underestimates the large manufacturing sector still present in developed economies. Including only primary activities in the mix ignores that agriculture employs very few people in advanced nations. Secondary and tertiary together correctly capture the industrial and service-dominated structure of developed economies.

A monocultural economy depends on a single agricultural commodity or raw material for export revenue, leaving little surplus capital to invest in industries, and making the economy vulnerable to price fluctuations. A multicultural economy, by contrast, produces diverse goods which supports capital accumulation needed for industrialisation. Capitalism as a system actually encourages private investment in industry and has driven industrialisation in many countries. A diversified economy, with income from multiple sectors, provides the broad base needed to finance industrial development.

Rapid population growth reduces the amount of land available per farmer, making it impossible to leave portions of land fallow for soil recovery as bush fallowing requires. Mechanised agriculture changes farming methods but is not widely accessible to most Nigerian smallholders and therefore cannot explain the widespread decline of fallowing. Availability of agricultural inputs like fertilisers reduces the need for fallowing but has not been distributed broadly enough to be the primary cause. Lack of interest in crop production contradicts the reality that most rural Nigerians still depend on farming for their livelihoods.

Subsistence farming involves growing food primarily for household consumption, and the majority of Nigeria's large rural population practises this form of agriculture for survival. Public service employment is concentrated in urban centres and accounts for a much smaller fraction of the workforce. Commercial farming requires capital investment and produces for the market, making it less accessible to most rural farmers. Trading is widespread in Nigeria but it remains secondary to subsistence agriculture as the dominant occupation of the majority.

Japan emerged as the world's second-largest manufacturing economy through rapid post-war industrialisation, technological innovation, and high productivity, ranking second only to the United States for much of the late twentieth century. Russia has significant industrial output but its manufacturing has not consistently ranked second globally. Germany is a major industrial power but ranks behind both the USA and Japan in overall manufacturing output. Britain was the world's first industrial nation but declined relatively as others grew, and does not hold second position.

The North Central Highland of Nigeria, which includes the Jos Plateau, reaches elevations of up to 1,500 metres above sea level, making it the highest region in the country. The Western Highland refers to the Yoruba hills and surrounding uplands which are lower in elevation. The Sokoto Plains are flat, low-lying sedimentary basins in the northwest of Nigeria. The Eastern Scarplands have notable elevations but the Jos Plateau in the north central region still represents the greatest heights.

Service buses, including the commercial minibuses and coaches commonly called danfos and molue in Nigerian cities, carry the largest number of passengers within urban areas and form the backbone of intra-city transport. Rail transport within Nigerian cities is negligible and not widely available to most residents. Taxis serve a portion of commuters but are more expensive and carry fewer people overall. Motorcycles became popular but at the time of the 2010 examination, service buses were recognised as the dominant mode for mass urban passenger movement.

At the time of the 2010 JAMB examination, Nigeria's population was widely estimated at approximately 140 million people based on projections from the 2006 national census. The figure of 124 million reflects older projections from around the early 2000s before the census. The 96 million figure corresponds to much earlier population estimates from the 1990s. The figure of 162 million is a more recent estimate that post-dates the 2010 examination year.

The Bakolori Irrigation Project in Zamfara State was developed partly to support large-scale cultivation of sugarcane alongside other crops, making it the most associated irrigation project with sugarcane production in Nigeria. Pategi is a town in Kwara State associated with agricultural activities but is not the primary irrigation project for sugarcane. Numan in Adamawa State hosts the Savannah Sugar Company but relies on its own specific water infrastructure. Shonga is known for commercial farming ventures introduced later and is not primarily associated with government-managed irrigation for sugarcane.

The concentration of industries in West African cities creates employment opportunities that attract large numbers of workers and their families from rural areas, directly driving high population density. Efficient transportation makes cities more accessible but follows rather than causes high population concentration. Social amenities such as schools and hospitals also attract people, but they are typically developed in response to existing population growth rather than being the primary cause. Administrative capitals attract civil servants and associated populations but this effect is smaller than industrial employment.

The southern coastlands of Nigeria, particularly the Niger Delta, suffer severely from oil pollution and spillage caused by decades of petroleum extraction activities, pipeline vandalism, and blowouts, which devastate farmland, water sources, and fishing grounds. Poor soil fertility is not the defining problem of this region, as the delta soils are naturally rich. Ocean tides are a natural phenomenon that coastal communities adapt to rather than a development problem. The terrain of the Niger Delta is predominantly flat and swampy, not hilly.

River Niger originates in the Futa Djallon highlands of Guinea and flows through the Guinea Highlands before entering Mali, making these highlands the source area of the river. The Plateau of Southern Mali is where the Niger forms its inland delta but is not the source of the river. The Adamawa Highlands are the source of River Benue, a major tributary of the Niger, not the Niger itself. The Mandara Mountains drain into the Lake Chad basin and do not feed the Niger River system.

South Africa possesses one of the richest gold deposits in the world, centred on the Witwatersrand reef in Gauteng, which made the country a dominant global gold producer for over a century. Limestone exists in South Africa but is not the country's defining or most economically significant mineral resource. Natural gas reserves in South Africa are limited compared to its solid mineral wealth. Copper is the major mineral resource of Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo, not South Africa.

In the equatorial region, intense solar radiation heats the surface strongly throughout the year, causing warm moist air to rise rapidly through convection, cool at higher altitudes, and condense into heavy afternoon rainfall, which is correctly termed convectional rainfall. Orographic rainfall results from air being forced upward over mountain barriers, which is not the primary mechanism in the flat equatorial lowlands. Harmattan winds originate from the Sahara and bring dry, dusty conditions, the opposite of rainfall. Cyclonic rainfall is associated with the collision of warm and cold air masses in mid-latitude regions, not the equatorial zone.

Among the listed atmospheric pollutants, nitrogen oxides are present in relatively smaller quantities compared to the others, making them the least in terms of volume of atmospheric pollution. Hydrocarbons are released in very large amounts from vehicle exhausts, industrial processes, and the burning of fossil fuels. Particulates include dust, soot, and smoke particles which are produced in enormous quantities from combustion and industrial activities. Sulphur oxides are emitted heavily from coal-burning power stations and industries and contribute significantly to acid rain formation.

Malaysia and Indonesia dominate global natural rubber production due to their hot, humid equatorial climate ideal for Hevea brasiliensis trees, while Liberia in West Africa hosts major rubber plantations, notably the historic Firestone plantation. These three nations together account for a huge share of world rubber output. Zimbabwe is a southern African country whose climate and economy are not suited for rubber cultivation. Niger is landlocked with a semi-arid Sahel climate, making rubber farming impossible there.

Western Europe, with industrial giants like Germany, the UK, and France, and the United States, with its massive manufacturing belt, together form the most developed and productive industrial regions on earth. These areas have centuries of industrial history, advanced technology, capital, and skilled labour. The Ruhr is only one industrial region within Germany and cannot represent an entire continental scale. Africa and the Caribbean are still developing, and while Japan is highly industrialised, Australia alone does not match the scale of Western Europe or the USA.

Ewekoro in Ogun State sits on extensive limestone deposits, which is the chief raw material for cement production, making proximity to raw materials the dominant location factor. Cement manufacturing is a weight-losing industry, so locating the factory at the raw material source reduces transport costs significantly. Water supply and transport infrastructure matter in any industry but are secondary here. Government policy may support industrialisation broadly but did not primarily determine this specific site.

Nomadic herders, predominantly the Fulani people, move their cattle, goats, and sheep across vast distances following seasonal rains and pasture, and this remains the dominant form of livestock rearing in Nigeria. The nomadic system suits the savanna regions where permanent water and pasture are seasonal. Sedentary and large-scale commercial ranching exists but is far less widespread. Smallholder farmers in Nigeria are mainly crop producers, not livestock specialists.

Lagos has the highest concentration of industries in Nigeria because it is the country's largest city, main seaport, and commercial nerve centre, providing access to imported raw materials, a massive consumer market, labour supply, and well-developed infrastructure. Industries gravitate to Lagos for easy export and import through Apapa and Tin Can Island ports. Kano and Kaduna have significant agro-processing industries but on a smaller scale. Port Harcourt is important for petroleum-related industries but does not match Lagos in overall industrial density.

South Africa dominates global gold production, particularly through the Witwatersrand Basin, making gold its historically major foreign exchange earner. Nigeria earns most of its foreign exchange from petroleum, not gold. Niger's primary export is uranium, while Tanzania exports gold in smaller quantities alongside other commodities.
