To find the length of a road on a map, you use a piece of string or strip of paper to follow the road's curves, then measure against the scale bar. Carefully tracing the major road through Ruwawa and converting using the map scale gives approximately 9km, making B correct. Options A (7km) and C (11km) result from under- or over-measuring the road's bends and curves. Precision in following winding roads is key, as straight-line distance will always underestimate actual road length.

Agriculture is the dominant economic activity in Ruwawa because the map shows extensive farmland, cultivation symbols, and rural settlement patterns typical of Nigerian agricultural communities. These land-use indicators far outweigh evidence of forestry reserves, major water extraction infrastructure, or dense transport networks. Forestry would require large forested areas with logging activity, while transportation becomes an economy driver only in major transit hubs. In most Nigerian rural map extracts at this level, widespread farmland makes agriculture the primary economic base.

Water transport is the cheapest mode of transportation because ships and barges can carry very large volumes of cargo using relatively little fuel per tonne-kilometre, with minimal infrastructure maintenance costs compared to roads and rail. Air transport is the most expensive due to high fuel consumption, aircraft maintenance, and airport costs. Road transport involves constant vehicle wear, fuel costs, and road maintenance, while rail requires expensive track infrastructure. For bulk goods over long distances, water remains globally and historically the most cost-effective option.

To calculate map area, you multiply the length by the width of the mapped area using the scale to convert map measurements to real-world distances. Applying the map scale to the grid squares or border measurements of this extract gives approximately 115 km², making C correct. Options A (95 km²) and B (105 km²) underestimate because of errors in reading the scale or boundary dimensions. Option D (125 km²) overestimates slightly, likely from including marginal areas outside the actual mapped content.

North of the major road, the surface reservoirs shown on the map have silted up or become waterlogged marshes, making them unreliable for drinking or irrigation. Because usable surface water is no longer available, residents depend on boreholes and wells that tap groundwater beneath the surface. Option A is wrong because plantations are not indicated as consuming surface water in that zone. Option C describes a symptom (boreholes exist) but not the reason why ground water is preferred over surface sources. Option D refers to diversion for the National Farm Project, which applies to a different part of the map area.

A flood plain forms when a river repeatedly overflows its banks and deposits alluvial sediment across a flat, low-lying area beside the channel, which matches the central landform on this map. The feature shows the characteristic flat terrain and proximity to a river typical of flood plains. A deltaic plain forms at a river's mouth where it meets the sea, which is not the case here. An outwash plain is created by glacial meltwater depositing material beyond a glacier, irrelevant to this West African context. An erosional plain results from long-term wearing down of highlands, producing a different landscape profile.

Bearing is measured clockwise from north (0°) at the starting point, which here is Adaba. Plotting a line from Adaba to Jata on the map and measuring the clockwise angle from the north line gives approximately 21°, placing Jata almost due north with a slight eastward deviation. A bearing of 17° would place Jata slightly closer to true north than the map evidence supports. Readings of 25° or 29° would push the direction too far east, misrepresenting the actual grid position of Jata relative to Adaba.

Settlements in this area cluster along or very close to the main road, indicating that ease of transportation and access to trade were the primary factors guiding where people chose to live. The main road enables movement of goods, people, and services, which is economically vital. Water transport is unlikely to dominate because no major navigable waterway runs through the settlement zone. While fertile land exists in the region, settlements did not spread uniformly across agricultural areas but instead hugged the road corridor. Defensive positioning against attack would produce hilltop or naturally protected sites, not roadside linear settlement patterns.

Line of sight to Bari Hill is blocked from position S because an intervening ridge or higher ground lies between S and the hill, preventing a direct visual connection. Intervisibility on a map is determined by drawing a cross-section and checking whether any terrain along the line of sight rises above the observer-to-target line. Positions P, Q, and R all have clear or sufficiently elevated sightlines that allow Bari Hill to be seen. At S, the ground in between is high enough to obstruct the view completely, making it the correct answer.

A rectilinear slope maintains a constant, uniform angle from top to bottom, appearing as a straight line on a cross-section profile. This is visible when contour lines are evenly spaced along the slope between X and Y. A convex slope curves outward with contours closer together at the base, while a concave slope curves inward with contours closer at the top. Stepped slopes show distinct breaks or terraces, which is not the case here.

Gradient is calculated by dividing the vertical interval (height difference) by the horizontal distance between two points. Reading from the map, the height difference between X and Y divided by the measured horizontal distance gives approximately 1:28. A ratio like 1:24 would indicate a steeper slope, while 1:30 would be gentler. Accurate map reading of both the contour values and the map scale is essential to arrive at the correct ratio.

A young population pyramid has a very broad base, indicating a large proportion of children and young people due to high birth rates. This pattern is typical of developing countries, including many African nations, where fertility rates remain high. An ageing population would show a narrower base and wider top, while a declining population has a base smaller than its middle. A stable population maintains roughly equal proportions across age groups.

Fluvial erosion refers to erosion carried out by rivers and running water, and hydraulic action and abrasion are its two key processes. Hydraulic action occurs when the sheer force and pressure of flowing water breaks apart and dislodges rock material, while abrasion happens when river-carried sediment scrapes and wears down the riverbed and banks. Aeolian erosion is wind-driven, glacial erosion involves ice, and karst erosion is chemical dissolution of limestone by slightly acidic water.

Kano State lies in the Sudan savanna zone of northern Nigeria, where the climate supports drought-tolerant grain crops like millet and sorghum alongside the famous groundnut cultivation. These crops thrive in the long dry season and moderate rainfall characteristic of that region. Potatoes and tea require cooler temperatures and higher rainfall, making them suited to highland areas like the Jos Plateau or southern Nigeria. Yam is predominantly a crop of the middle belt and southern states.

Reading the contour lines and spot heights on the map extract, the highest elevation recorded in the region falls just above 100 metres above mean sea level, making option A correct. Options B, C, and D suggest higher values (110m, 120m, 130m), but no contour line or spot height on the map reaches those levels. When interpreting topographic maps, always trace the highest numbered contour or spot height carefully before choosing an answer.

Intervisibility between two points depends on whether any higher ground lies along the line of sight between them. Triangulation station 105 cannot be seen from the quarry edge because intervening high ground or a ridge blocks the direct line of sight. Stations 82, 94, and 96 are positioned such that the terrain between them and the quarry edge is lower, allowing an unobstructed view. Always draw an imaginary straight line between two points and check for any obstruction on the cross-section when testing intervisibility.

A population structure with a very wide base (many young people) and a narrow top (few elderly) produces a high dependency ratio, meaning a large proportion of non-working young people depend on a small working-age population. Option A is wrong because a wide base means most people are children, not yet productive workers. Option C is incorrect because a youthful population actually demands higher investment in schools, hospitals, and other social services, not lower. Option D does not apply since high life expectancy is associated with an aging population, not a youthful one.

A nodal settlement pattern is one where settlements cluster around a central point, such as a road junction, market, or administrative centre, with smaller settlements radiating outward from that node. The map shows this arrangement, making D the best description. Nucleated means buildings are tightly packed together but does not imply a central hub with radiating offshoots. Dispersed means settlements are scattered randomly, while linear means they follow a straight feature like a road or river, neither of which matches the pattern shown.

A broken ridge is an irregular, discontinuous elevated landform where the high ground is interrupted by gaps, depressions, or valleys, and the contour lines on the map between River Oni and the Kedi-Ibaga road show exactly this uneven, fragmented high ground. A rolling plain would show gently undulating, low-relief terrain with widely spaced contours. A cuesta has one gentle slope and one steep escarpment and results from differential erosion of tilted rock layers. A fault-scarp is a sharp, straight cliff produced by faulting, which the contour pattern in this area does not suggest.

Footslopes are the preferred settlement sites because they offer a middle ground — high enough to avoid flooding from the river below, yet low enough to access water and fertile soils nearby. Valley floors and flood plains are too prone to seasonal flooding for safe habitation. Ridge tops are exposed, windy, and difficult to build on. Footslopes thus balance safety, water access, and buildable terrain.

Measuring River Kudi along its winding course using the map's scale gives approximately 20km. Map distance measurement requires following every bend of the river with a piece of string or dividers, then converting using the given scale. Options like 22km overestimate and 16km underestimate the traced length. Accurate scale conversion is the key skill being tested here.

A broad, shallow channel is characteristic of a river flowing across a gentle, low-lying flood plain where there is little gradient to drive downward erosion. Incised channels are deeply cut into bedrock, typical of steep upland areas — the opposite of this landscape. A U-shaped valley is formed by glacial action, not river processes in Nigeria. Graded describes the river's equilibrium profile, not its physical cross-section shape.

A flood plain is a low, flat area built up by river sediment deposits during repeated floods, and the broad, meandering River Kudi with its shallow channel confirms this landscape type. A high plain sits at elevated altitude with no major active river shaping it. A pediplain forms in arid climates through slope retreat, not the humid conditions implied here. A peneplain is an ancient, almost flat erosion surface — far older and more featureless than what an active river system like this produces.

Settlements on footslopes near a flood plain face poor accessibility because roads crossing the low-lying flood plain are frequently submerged or waterlogged during rainy seasons, cutting communities off. Poor drainage is more directly a problem for settlements built on the valley floor itself, not the footslopes. Dense vegetation and infertile soils are not the defining challenge here — flood plains are actually known for fertile alluvial soils. Isolation caused by flooded routes is the dominant practical problem.

Grid references are read by going across first (easting) then up (northing), so 098172 means easting 098 and northing 172. Maga is the settlement located at that exact coordinate intersection on the map. Dan, Biu, and Bika each fall at different grid coordinates and would give different easting or northing readings when traced correctly on the topographic map.

African rivers are largely unnavigable because their courses drop sharply as they descend from high interior plateaus to coastal plains, creating numerous rapids and waterfalls that block boat movement. The Niger, Congo, and Zambezi all have famous falls and cataracts that interrupt navigation. Low water volume affects only some rivers seasonally, and African rivers like the Congo are actually among the world's longest, so length is not the issue. Seasonality affects some rivers but is not the primary continent-wide barrier.

The Gezira Plains in Sudan, lying between the Blue and White Nile rivers, is one of Africa's largest and most famous irrigation schemes, using canal water from the Sennar Dam. The Southern Sudan and Zaire Basin receive heavy rainfall and do not rely on irrigation agriculture. The Great Rift Valley is known for tectonic activity and some pastoralism but is not a major irrigation zone.

Contour lines on a topographic map show elevation, and the highest point in an area lies above the value of the highest closed contour ring shown. If the highest drawn contour is 375m and the hill summit lies within it but above it, the peak exceeds 375m. Options A, B, and C represent lower contour values that the summit has already surpassed, making 375m the minimum threshold the highest point exceeds.

West Africa's climate is controlled by two opposing air masses: the Tropical Continental (cT) air mass, which originates over the Sahara and brings the dry, dusty Harmattan wind, and the Tropical Maritime (mT) air mass, which originates over the Atlantic Ocean and brings moist, rain-bearing southwest winds. Their interplay along the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) determines wet and dry seasons. Option A confuses wind names with air mass names, and options B and D include incorrect or redundant classifications not used in standard West African climatology.

When a river deposits alluvium (sediment) on its bed over many years, the valley floor rises and the channel becomes shallower. This reduced depth means the river holds less water before spilling over its banks, making flooding far more likely. Rainfall alone (option B) can raise water volume but does not explain chronic overflow — the root cause is the loss of channel depth. A narrow valley (D) would confine water vertically, not cause it to spill, and farm waste blocking (C) is a minor human activity, not a geographic explanation.

Less rugged, flatter terrain to the south makes construction, farming, and transportation easier, naturally attracting more settlers. Fertile northern land being reserved for farming (A) is illogical — fertile land typically attracts settlement, not repels it. Flooding liability in the north (B) is contradicted by the map's drainage patterns. River blindness (D) is a health factor relevant in some West African contexts but is not the primary geographic reason visible on this map.

This is a map-reading exercise requiring students to trace the Owa River from its source to its terminus and convert that distance using the map's scale. Careful measurement yields approximately 19 km. Options B, C, and D (20, 23, 25 km) result from inaccurate tracing or misapplication of the scale — common errors include not following every meander of the river or misreading the scale bar.

Note: The description in this question — salty white surface crusts in arid regions — is the textbook definition of Solonchak soils (option A), and most geography authorities classify it that way. Podzols (D) are actually found in cool, humid climates like boreal forests, with a bleached ash-grey leached horizon, not salt crusts. Solonetz soils are also salt-affected but have a columnar structure, while Chernozem are the dark fertile grassland soils. Students should be aware this question's answer key likely contains an error — the soil described is Solonchak.

Sudan's Gezira scheme — the massive irrigation project between the Blue and White Nile rivers — has made irrigated cotton the backbone of its agricultural economy for over a century. No other country on the list depends on irrigated cotton to the same extent. Mali grows some cotton but relies mainly on rainfed agriculture. Zimbabwe's economy has historically centred on tobacco and maize, while Uganda's key export crop is coffee, not cotton.

Aperi is a wet point settlement because it is located close to a reliable water source, making water easily accessible to its inhabitants. Wet point settlements historically developed where people needed guaranteed water supply for domestic use and farming. A dry point settlement sits on elevated or well-drained land specifically to avoid flooding or waterlogging, which is the opposite of Aperi's situation. A confluence town forms where two rivers meet, while a foothill settlement is found at the base of hills, neither of which describes Aperi's defining characteristic.

From the temperature graph, only 5 months record temperatures above the annual mean temperature line. When you draw a horizontal line at the average temperature across the year, you count each month whose bar or point rises above that line. Students often overcount by including months that appear close to but not actually above the mean. Careful reading of the graph shows that 6, 7, or 8 months do not cross the mean threshold, making 5 the correct count.

Station Y records a December temperature of -4°C, indicating it lies in a high-latitude location where winter months bring sub-zero temperatures. December falls in the Northern Hemisphere winter, so stations at higher latitudes experience freezing conditions at that time. Options like 24°C or 32°C would represent tropical or hot conditions completely inconsistent with a December reading at Station Y on the graph. A reading of 4°C is close but still above freezing, which does not match the value plotted for Station Y in December.

The Benguela Current is a cold ocean current that flows northward along the western coast of southern Africa, originating from the Antarctic region. On maps of African ocean currents, it is positioned off the coasts of Namibia and South Africa on the Atlantic side. Current 3 on the map corresponds to this cold northward-flowing current on the southwestern Atlantic coast. The other numbered currents represent different currents such as the warm Mozambique or Agulhas currents on the eastern side, or other Atlantic currents that do not match the Benguela's position and direction.

Reclamation is most appropriate around Aperi because, as a wet point settlement near waterlogged or marshy terrain, the land needs to be drained and reclaimed for productive use. Reclamation involves converting swampy or flooded land into usable farmland or habitable ground. Terracing and contour ploughing are designed for sloping hillside land to prevent erosion, not flat, waterlogged areas. Afforestation addresses soil erosion and desert encroachment rather than the drainage problems associated with a wet point settlement like Aperi.

The Ahaggar (Hoggar) plateau is a high mountainous region located in the central Sahara Desert within southern Algeria. On maps of North Africa used in JAMB, it is typically marked at position Q, sitting in the interior of Algeria. Options P, R, and S represent other geographic regions such as coastal lowlands, the Atlas Mountains, or the Sudan savanna zone, none of which correspond to the Ahaggar plateau's central Saharan position.

Rivers flowing through highland plateau areas like Ahaggar have steep gradients and fast-moving water, giving them the energy to cut vertically downward into the land — this is called down-cutting or vertical erosion. Lateral erosion and deposition are characteristic of rivers in their lower, flatter middle and old-age stages where velocity decreases. Terracing is a landform result of river rejuvenation, not a primary river activity. The high elevation and steep slopes of a plateau make down-cutting the dominant process.

Ubi, as shown on the map, displays features such as roads, a school, and a market, which indicate transportation links, educational facilities, and commercial activity as its main functions. Option A is wrong because no church/mosque or hospital symbol dominates the settlement. Option C is wrong because manufacturing requires industrial symbols not typical of a small settlement like Ubi. Option D is incorrect because while farming and education may be present, transportation is a stronger function given the road networks shown.

Reading the contour map, the rest house located north-east of Jeta sits on or very close to the 50-metre contour line, making 50m the correct approximate height. Contour interpolation between surrounding lines confirms the elevation is closest to 50m rather than 30m, 40m, or 45m. Students must trace the contour lines carefully outward from the rest house symbol to identify which contour it lies on or nearest to.

A dendritic drainage pattern resembles the branching of a tree, with tributaries joining the main river at acute angles, and it develops on uniform or homogeneous rock where no structural control guides the streams. The Gindi river basin shows this irregular tree-branch pattern. Rectangular drainage forms on heavily jointed or faulted rock, radial drainage spreads outward from a central high point like a volcanic cone, and trellis drainage forms where hard and soft rock bands alternate in parallel — none of these structural controls apply to the Gindi basin.

Monsoon climate is marked by a distinct reversal of wind direction that produces one very wet season and one pronounced dry season, which matches the pattern shown in the graph. Equatorial climate has rainfall distributed throughout the year with no true dry season, so it does not fit. Mediterranean climate has its rainfall concentrated in the cooler winter months, the opposite of what monsoon regions experience. Montane climate is controlled by altitude rather than seasonal wind shifts, making it unsuitable here.

Poor transport network is the best explanation because without accessible roads and routes, people cannot move goods to markets, reach services, or attract economic activity, making an area unattractive for settlement. Rough topography and dense forest can discourage settlement, but the map of the Gindi river basin does not indicate these as the dominant feature. Scarcity of farmland would actually push people away from agriculture but does not on its own account for low settlement density across a whole basin. Transport access is consistently the strongest pull or push factor for settlement patterns in Nigerian geography.

To find road length on a map, you measure the route carefully with a string or piece of thread along all bends and curves, then straighten it against the map's scale bar to convert to real distance. The main road from Robo Junction to Oseb Junction, when measured this way, gives approximately 6.5 km. Students who get higher values like 8.5 km or 9.5 km usually make the error of measuring a straight-line distance rather than following the actual winding road. Always trace the road faithfully, including every curve, before reading off the distance.

Annual range of temperature is calculated by subtracting the lowest monthly temperature from the highest monthly temperature on the graph. The graph shows temperatures staying fairly close together across the year, giving a range of approximately 4°C. Options C (24°C) and D (28°C) are mistakes students make when they read off an actual temperature value instead of calculating the difference between highest and lowest. Option B (8°C) overestimates the spread between the maximum and minimum monthly values shown.

Relative relief is found by subtracting the lowest contour value on the map from the highest contour value, giving the total height difference across the mapped area. The map shows a highest point and a lowest point whose difference is slightly above 575 m, making D correct. Options A (75 m) and B (105 m) are far too small and would suggest nearly flat terrain, which contradicts the contour pattern on the map. Option C (485 m) falls short of the actual difference between the extreme contour lines shown.

Farming is the dominant human activity in most rural areas of Nigeria and West Africa, especially where the land is flat and fertile enough to support crops. The map symbols typically show cultivated land, settlements, and paths connecting farms, all pointing to agricultural activity. Fishing requires proximity to significant water bodies, lumbering requires dense forest reserves, and ranching requires vast open grasslands — none of which dominate the described area. Where you see small scattered settlements and cleared vegetation on a topographic map, subsistence or commercial farming is the most logical conclusion.

Roads are built along watersheds — the high ridges separating river valleys — because these areas are well-drained, relatively flat, and avoid the flooding and swampy conditions found in valley floors. Engineers prefer watersheds as natural highways since they provide firm ground and easier construction compared to steep or wet terrain. Steep slopes make road construction dangerous and expensive, while valley floors and gentle slopes near rivers are prone to waterlogging and floods. Hilltops are often too narrow and exposed, making them impractical for road routing.

Stippled coastal seas on world maps represent areas of commercial fishing, where large-scale, mechanized fishing operations harvest fish for sale and export. These include the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, the North Sea, and waters off Japan and Peru — all major commercial fishing zones. Fish farming is an inland or coastal pond activity, not an open-sea operation. Whaling is highly restricted today and was never the primary use of these broad coastal zones. Deep sea fishing occurs in the open ocean far from coasts, while these stippled areas are specifically coastal shelf regions.

South East Asia, particularly countries like Vietnam, Bangladesh, and Indonesia, is famous for intensive peasant farming — small landholders working every available piece of land to produce rice and other food crops, which is why these areas can support such enormous populations. The region actually exports rice rather than importing it massively, making option A wrong. Birth and death rates in South East Asia have historically been high, not low, ruling out option C. Heavy industries are concentrated in specific urban zones like China's coastal cities, not spread across the densely populated rural farming areas.

The shaded areas numbered 1–6 on the world population map represent sparsely populated regions — places like the Sahara Desert, Amazon Basin, Siberia, Central Australia, Arctic tundra, and the Himalayas, all of which are inhospitable to large human settlement. These regions are not simply biological deserts, as some contain rich biodiversity despite low human populations. Nomadic grazing occurs in some of these zones but is not the defining characteristic of all six areas. While some areas contain mountains, not all are mountainous — the common link is their very low population density due to harsh climates, poor soils, or extreme terrain.

Japan is the major Pacific country shown, and it is globally renowned for exporting automobiles (Toyota, Honda, Nissan), electronics (Sony, Panasonic, Toshiba), and skilled manpower. Option A is wrong because Japan imports crude oil rather than exporting it, as the country has very limited petroleum reserves. Option C is partially correct with electronics but fish is not a major export commodity in the same category. Option D is wrong because Japan does not export iron ore in significant quantities; it actually imports iron ore for its steel industry.

A flood plain with a monadnock correctly describes an area where a large flat lowland formed by river deposition exists alongside an isolated hill or residual rock mass rising sharply above it. A plateau with a broad footslope plain implies elevated flat land which does not match a predominantly low-lying depositional surface. An undulating high plain with inselbergs would suggest a generally elevated surface with scattered hills, while a rugged hill with a pediment slope implies steep, rough terrain rather than a flat alluvial setting.

Using the map scale provided, measuring the broad and shallow section of River Amy from where it widens to where it narrows again gives an approximate distance of 7.3km. Option A (5.3km) underestimates the length of this section, likely from miscounting grid squares or misreading the scale. Options C and D (12.8km and 15.0km) significantly overestimate by extending the measurement beyond the clearly defined broad-shallow segment into adjacent river sections.

When River Amy descends from highland and reaches the base of a hill, the gradient flattens sharply, causing the river to lose its velocity and energy, so it can no longer carry its sediment load and deposits it. Option A is wrong because no dam is indicated on the map in that location. Option C contradicts the process since increased erosive power would remove rather than deposit material. Option D (channelization) is a human modification that would actually increase flow speed and reduce deposition rather than cause it.

Slope is the dominant factor controlling settlement distribution in this area because people avoid building on steep or unstable terrain and instead concentrate on gentle or flat slopes that allow safe construction and easy movement. Drainage can influence settlement but slope determines where drainage itself occurs, making it the more fundamental factor here. Vegetation and soils are secondary factors that respond to slope and other physical conditions rather than directly dictating where clusters of settlements form on the map.

Nigeria has four major oil refineries located in Port Harcourt (two), Warri, and Kaduna — these are the sites typically marked with solid triangles on JAMB geography maps of Nigeria. Thermal power stations are found at places like Sapele, Egbin, and Kainji, not the same locations. International airports and automobile assembly plants occupy entirely different sites and are fewer in number than the triangles shown.

Humus-rich soils retain moisture and supply nutrients that support the growth and maintenance of woodland vegetation. Low lumbering activity might preserve existing trees but cannot cause woodland to develop in the first place. Orographic rainfall benefits vegetation broadly but does not specifically explain woodland on its own, and steep gradients typically hinder, not promote, dense vegetation growth.

The shaded areas labelled Y correspond to major river floodplains in Nigeria — particularly along the River Niger and River Benue — where seasonal flooding creates ideal waterlogged conditions for rice cultivation. Dry season wheat is grown in irrigated areas of the far north, not floodplains. Large-scale irrigation farming is associated with drier northern river valleys, while fish farming, though practised near rivers, is not the dominant land use for which these floodplain zones are specifically noted.

When a winding road on a map is measured carefully using a piece of string or a map measurer along its curves and then converted with the given scale, the distance works out to approximately 9.2 km. Options like 8.0 km and 8.6 km underestimate the road length because they fail to account fully for the bends and curves along the route. 9.8 km overshoots the correct measurement, likely from over-tracing the curves.

The area labelled Z represents Nigeria's far north — states like Sokoto, Yobe, Borno, and Kebbi — which lie at the southern edge of the Sahara Desert and experience advancing desertification, prolonged droughts, and severe land degradation. River blindness (onchocerciasis) is linked to fast-flowing rivers in the middle belt and south, not the arid north. Tsetse fly infestation thrives in humid forest and savanna zones, while toxic waste pollution is an urban and oil-producing delta problem.

Drainage is the major constraint because areas with rivers, swamps, or waterlogged soils make road construction extremely difficult and expensive — foundations become unstable and roads flood easily. Vegetation (A) can be cleared with machinery, and settlement patterns (C) can be worked around during road planning. Terrain (D) presents challenges but can be overcome with cuts and fills; drainage problems however require costly culverts, bridges, and embankments throughout. In many Nigerian lowland or riverine map extracts, crossing drainage channels repeatedly is the dominant engineering obstacle.

Bearings are measured clockwise from north, so 160° places Y in a south-southeast direction from X. Reading the map carefully, the line from X to Y falls between due south (180°) and southeast (135°), closer to south, giving approximately 160°. Option A (155°) and C (165°) are too far off after careful protractor reading. Option D (170°) would be nearly due south, which does not match the angle shown on the map extract.

Low islands and sand banks form when a river loses velocity and deposits its sediment load, which only happens in shallow water where the current is too weak to keep material in suspension. A deep channel (A) maintains strong flow that scours the bed and prevents deposition. An eroding channel (B) would show undercutting of banks and removal of material, not deposition. Navigable channels (D) must be deep and clear of obstructions, so the presence of sand banks actually rules out navigation for large vessels.

Gradient is calculated as vertical interval divided by horizontal distance, expressed as a ratio like 1:n. Working from the map, the road descending the spur into Bobo town covers a relatively long horizontal distance for its vertical drop, giving the gentlest ratio of 1:52 among the options. Options A (1:37), B (1:42), and C (1:47) all represent steeper gradients — a smaller second number means more rise per unit of horizontal distance. Carefully measuring the road length and counting the contour crossings on the map confirms 1:52 as the correct approximation.

Arctic climate is defined by extreme cold throughout the year — temperatures here reach -22°C in winter and barely rise above 5°C even in the warmest months, with precipitation low and spread thinly. Siberian (B) climate is also very cold and continental but typically shows a stronger summer warming pulse and is associated specifically with interior Asia. Laurentian (A) climate occurs in northeastern North America and Canada with milder winters and higher precipitation. Steppe (D) is semi-arid with moderate seasonal temperatures, completely inconsistent with the sub-zero readings shown in this data.

A drawbridge is specifically designed to allow road vehicles and motorists to cross a river, making it the correct choice for motorists travelling between Bobo and Achira. A ferry also carries vehicles but is typically used for wider crossings and operates on a schedule, making it less likely on a mapped local route. Boats are for passengers, not vehicles, and ships require deep navigable water unsuitable for a small river crossing between two settlements.

Drainage is the dominant factor controlling where cultivation occurs on the map because crops can only grow on well-drained land, while waterlogged or flood-prone areas remain uncultivated. The pattern of farmland closely follows areas away from rivers and marshy zones, confirming drainage as the primary influence. Settlement and roads tend to follow where cultivation already exists, not the other way around, and climate is uniform across such a small mapped area so it cannot explain local variation in farming distribution.

An embankment is required when a road must be built across low-lying, marshy, or depressed ground by piling up earth to raise the road above the surrounding terrain. The area between Achira and Gara lies in a low or flat zone, so the road needs to be elevated. A cutting is the opposite situation, used when a road passes through a hill or ridge. A tunnel is for passing through solid mountains, and a levee is a flood-control structure, neither of which applies here.

Aperi is a wet-point settlement because it is located close to a water source such as a river or stream, which historically attracted human settlement for drinking water and agriculture. Dry-point settlements are positioned on higher ground specifically to avoid flooding and waterlogging, the opposite of Aperi's location. A confluence settlement sits at the meeting point of two rivers, while a foothill settlement is found at the base of a highland area, neither of which describes Aperi's position on the map.

A straight slope is characterised by evenly spaced contour lines, meaning the gradient is uniform from top to bottom, and the profile along LK shows this regular spacing. A convex slope has contour lines that are closer together near the bottom and wider apart near the top, producing a curved outward profile. A concave slope is the reverse, with lines closer at the top, and a convex-concave slope combines both features, none of which match the even spacing seen along the LK transect.

To find the distance between two confluences along River Kedi, you measure the winding river path between both points using a thread or dividers, then apply the map scale to convert to real-world distance. Working through this calculation with the given map gives approximately 10.7 km. Option A (9.7 km) underestimates because it may follow a straighter path than the actual river course. Options C and D overestimate the distance by not accounting for the correct scale conversion.

A spur is a narrow, tongue-like projection of high land that extends outward from a main hill or highland into lower surrounding terrain, and on a contour map its contours form a V-shape pointing downhill. A feature running NW to SE that projects from higher ground fits this definition exactly. A ridge is broader and forms a continuous elevated line rather than a projection. An escarpment is a steep cliff-like slope, while an embankment is an artificial raised structure built by humans, neither of which describes this natural landform.

Prismatic compass survey uses precise magnetic bearings and measured distances to locate points accurately, and when combined with leveling it produces detailed, accurate contoured maps even over small areas. Its instruments reduce human error in direction measurement significantly compared to other field methods. Chain survey only measures distances and cannot directly record elevation data needed for contours. Plane-table survey is fast but relies on visual estimation and is less precise. Land-use survey records vegetation and activity types, not relief.

Continentality is the climatic effect of being far from the moderating influence of the ocean, producing extreme heat, very low rainfall, and prolonged dry seasons. The Chad Basin in northeast Nigeria is the farthest inland of all the options, making it most affected by this harsh continental climate, which drives desertification, drought, and poor agricultural conditions that stunt economic growth. The Niger Delta and Cross River Basin are coastal or near-coastal, so maritime air masses keep their climates wetter and more stable. The Niger-Benue Trough also receives more rainfall from converging river systems.

Intervisibility between two points on a map is determined by drawing a cross-section along the line connecting them and checking whether any intervening high ground breaks the line of sight. Tap is visible from Enso because no ridge or hill of sufficient height lies between them to obstruct the direct sightline. From Klo, Nino, and Ned, intervening terrain creates obstructions that would block the view to Tap. This type of question tests your ability to read contour lines and interpret relative heights along a given profile.

Spot heights on topographic maps mark the exact elevation of a point, and reading the contour lines surrounding the eastern peak places it closest to 725m above sea level. Options like 710m and 695m correspond to lower contour intervals on the map, not the peak itself. 715m is a plausible distractor but does not align with the marked spot height value. Always read spot height figures directly — they are printed beside the dot on the map.

Bearing is measured clockwise from north (000°), so a bearing of 350° means nearly due north with a slight westward lean. Ned lies roughly north-northwest of the road junction at Gag, giving a bearing close to 350°. A bearing of 80° would place Ned almost due east, while 170° points south-southeast and 260° points west — none of these match the map layout. Always draw a north line at the reference point and measure clockwise to the target.

Steep hill slopes make road construction and settlement development difficult and expensive, so communities avoid building in such terrain. The map shows closely spaced contour lines in that area, confirming steep gradients. Mining activities and rivers could limit land use but are not the dominant factor shown here. Footpaths are a symptom of restricted movement, not a cause of it.

Straight-line distance (as the crow flies) is measured using a ruler on the map and then converted using the map scale; applying the given scale between the trigonometrical station and Josan yields approximately 6.5km. Options of 5.0km and 5.5km underestimate the distance visible on the map, while 6.0km falls just short of the correct measurement. Precision in placing the ruler at the exact centre of both symbols is critical for accurate results.

Rice thrives in low-lying, waterlogged or flood-prone areas such as river basins and deltas, making it perfectly suited to the lower basin of River Madu where water is abundant and soils are seasonally saturated. Groundnut and cotton require well-drained sandy or loamy soils and cannot tolerate waterlogging. Coffee needs highland, humid conditions with good drainage, not a river basin floor. River lower basins in West Africa are classic rice-growing zones studied extensively in JAMB geography.

A ridge is an elongated elevated landform that runs in a linear direction, which matches a feature trending north to north-east. Trigonometrical stations are typically placed on ridges because their linear elevation makes them ideal for surveying. A conical hill is a rounded, isolated peak, not a linear feature. A cliff is a steep vertical face, while a plateau is a flat-topped elevated area — neither fits a directional linear feature on a contour map.

On a topographic map, the highest point is identified by reading the contour values, and the spot height or highest closed contour in this map area reads 320m. Option A (300m) and B (250m) represent lower contour lines visible on the map. Option D (275m) is also a lower elevation than the peak. Always trace contour lines outward from the centre of a hill — the innermost closed contour carries the highest value.

The north-western part of the map area shows dense forest or woodland symbols, indicating lumbering (timber extraction) as the dominant economic activity. Mining would require mineral deposit symbols or pit markings on the map. Mixed farming and animal husbandry are associated with open grassland or farmland symbols, not forested terrain. When vegetation cover on a map is dense, lumbering is the logical economic activity to infer.

The length of the secondary road is calculated by using the map's scale — measuring the road with a piece of string or ruler along its bends and curves, then converting using the representative fraction. The winding nature of secondary roads means the actual distance is longer than a straight-line estimate, giving approximately 13.5km. Options A, B, and D underestimate the road length because they do not fully account for all the curves and bends along the route.

An embankment is a raised road constructed above the surrounding low-lying floodplain, allowing traffic to cross without being submerged during flooding. This is the standard engineering solution in Nigerian road construction across river floodplains. A flyover spans obstacles using columns and is used over roads or valleys, not flood plains. An underground passage would be impractical in waterlogged terrain, and a road cutting involves digging into elevated ground, which is the opposite of what a floodplain requires.

Downstream, river gradient becomes gentle and velocity slows, causing the river to swing sideways and form wide bends called meanders. River Haba below the bridge shows this characteristic winding pattern typical of a river's lower course. A levee is a raised embankment built up by flood deposits along the bank, not a channel shape. A knick point is a sudden break in gradient found in the middle course, while braiding occurs when a river splits into multiple shallow channels due to excessive sediment load.

The map shows an area with scattered rural settlements, open land, and few industrial or water features, pointing strongly to farming as the dominant livelihood. Farming is the most common occupation in rural Nigerian communities and the land use pattern on the map supports this. Fishing requires prominent rivers, lakes, or coastal proximity. Lumbering needs dense forest reserves, and mining requires visible mineral extraction sites or ore-bearing geology, none of which dominate the mapped area.

Two settlements are intervisible when a straight line drawn between them on the map passes over no higher ground, meaning you can see directly from one to the other. Bikun and Abuojo share a line of sight with no intervening ridge or hill blocking the view based on the contour pattern. The other pairs, such as Abuojo and Hua or Miki and Abuojo, have elevated ground between them that would obstruct direct vision. Always check contour lines between two points to determine intervisibility.

To find students scoring between 6% and 60%, read the cumulative frequency values for both marks from the ogive curve, then subtract. The cumulative frequency at 60% minus the cumulative frequency at 6% gives the students in that score range, which equals 70. Option B (66) and C (62) result from misreading the curve at one endpoint. Option D (58) under-reads both values, giving a smaller difference than the correct reading.

To award scholarships to the top 10% of students, find the mark at the 90th percentile on the cumulative frequency curve. Locate 90% of the total students on the vertical axis, draw a horizontal line to the curve, then drop vertically to read off the corresponding mark, which gives 78%. Option A (86%) and B (82%) are too high and correspond to percentiles above 90. Option D (74%) falls below the 90th percentile, meaning more than 10% of students scored above it.

From the map of Nuriki District, calculating the total land area by counting grid squares and applying the map scale gives 300 sq km. Option A (290 sq km) and C (310 sq km) arise from miscounting partial grid squares at the district boundary. Option D (320 sq km) significantly overestimates the area. Accurate grid-square counting with careful treatment of boundary squares is the key skill tested here.

Farming is the most important economic activity because the map shows extensive farmland symbols covering the majority of Nuriki District's land area. Fishing would only dominate in coastal or riverine communities where water bodies are the primary feature. Mining and lumbering require specific map symbols such as mine shafts or dense forest cover, which are not prominently featured. The dominance of cultivated land symbols on the map makes farming the clear answer.

All settlements in the map are plotted on hilltops, which is a common settlement pattern in areas where communities sought defensive advantage and avoided flooding. Floodplains (Option D) are the low-lying areas along rivers that flood seasonally, making them unsuitable for permanent settlement. Steep slopes (Option C) are unstable and difficult to build on. Hilltop settlement reflects both security and practical drainage advantages that communities historically preferred.

The steepest part of the area has no settlements because the gradient is too high for safe and practical habitation. Very steep terrain makes construction of buildings and roads extremely difficult and dangerous. Option D (prone to erosion) is a consequence of steepness rather than the primary reason settlers avoid it. Option A (lacks roads) is itself caused by the steepness, so it is an effect not a cause. Excessive height and gradient is the fundamental deterrent to settlement.

Measuring along the road route from Zara to Lime on the map using a string or dividers, then applying the map scale, gives approximately 10 km. Road distance is always longer than straight-line distance because roads curve around hills and other obstacles. Options A (4 km) and B (6 km) reflect straight-line or under-measured estimates that ignore the winding nature of the road. Option D (8 km) is close but still underestimates the full length of the road as it curves across the map.

Farming is the correct second occupation because the map shows open lowland areas typical of agricultural land alongside the river or water body that supports fishing. Lumbering requires dense tropical forest which is not indicated in this area. Manufacturing needs industrial infrastructure not shown on the map. Mining requires mineral deposits which, if present, would make that the dominant activity rather than a secondary one alongside fishing.

Zara town sits in the northeast portion of the map when you locate it relative to the map's central reference point and use the compass bearing. In map reading, direction is always measured from a known central or southern reference toward the feature in question. The southeast, southwest, and northwest options place Zara in quadrants that do not match its grid coordinates on the 2016 JAMB map extract.

Gradient is calculated as vertical interval divided by horizontal distance, expressed as a ratio. Measuring from the centre of Zafi to the bridge over River Saga on this map gives a rise of 1 unit for every 68 units of horizontal distance, making 1:68 correct. Options like 1:65 or 1:62 represent steeper gradients, while 1:59 is steeper still — all inconsistent with the measured height difference and map distance between those two points.

To find total map area, you multiply the map's length by its width after converting the measurements using the given scale. On this JAMB extract, the calculation yields approximately 288 square kilometres. The other options — 278, 258, and 268 square kilometres — result from measurement errors or incorrect scale conversion when computing the grid dimensions.

Railways in West Africa were historically built by colonial administrations primarily to move minerals from inland extraction sites to coastal ports for export, and this map shows evidence of mineral deposits in the region. Passengers travel more efficiently by road over short distances, and farm produce is bulky but was rarely the sole justification for expensive railway construction. Forest products similarly do not explain the railway's route, which aligns with mineral-rich terrain on the map.

Figu and Ligo are visible from the trigonometrical station because they occupy elevated ground with no major physical barriers interrupting the line of sight between them and the station. A trigonometrical station is itself placed on high ground, so only features at comparable or unobstructed elevations can be seen from it. Kileko and Pom lie in lower or sheltered positions where intervening relief blocks visibility. Ligo alone or Pom alone paired with other options would mix visible and invisible features, making those combinations incorrect.

Dispersed settlement means homesteads and buildings are widely scattered across the landscape with no clustering, which matches the eastern part of this map where settlements appear spread far apart. Nucleated settlement would show a tight cluster of buildings around a centre such as a market or road junction. Linear settlement follows a line such as a road or river, while conurbation refers to merged urban areas — neither pattern fits a rural eastern zone with scattered compounds.

Measuring River Maya along its entire course on the map, accounting for its bends and meanders using a piece of string or divider intervals, and then converting with the map scale gives approximately 7.5 km. Straight-line distance would underestimate the true length because rivers curve. Options like 5.5 km and 6.5 km are too short and likely result from measuring only part of the river or ignoring its bends, while 8.5 km overshoots the actual measured distance.

The presence of a river, creek, or water body prominently featured on the map, combined with settlement patterns near the water, points strongly to fishing as the dominant economic activity. Farming would be supported by evidence of farmland or cultivation symbols, which are not the dominant feature here. Lumbering requires dense forest cover as the primary land use, and pastoralism needs open grassland with animal grazing symbols — neither dominates the map evidence for this area.

Bearing is measured clockwise from North, and La'ah lies to the northwest of Gambo, giving a bearing of 300 degrees. A bearing of 60 degrees would place La'ah to the northeast of Gambo, which is the opposite direction. 30 degrees is nearly due north with a slight eastward lean, and 120 degrees points to the southeast — both contradict the northwest position of La'ah relative to Gambo on the map.

Kondo sits in a gap, which is a low-lying opening or pass between higher ground such as hills or ridges. Gaps form where rivers or erosion cut through elevated terrain, and settlements often develop there because they serve as natural route-ways. A ridge is an elongated high point, a scarp is a steep slope face, and a hill is an isolated raised landform — none of these describe a low passage between high ground where Kondo is located.

Areas below the 105-metre contour represent the lowest ground on the map, typically valley floors or flood plains where water naturally collects during heavy rains. Seasonal flooding is concentrated here because water drains downslope and accumulates in these depressions. Higher areas like those above 120 metres or between the 105 and 135 metre contours sit on elevated ground where floodwater drains away rather than pooling.

A dissected plateau is revealed when contours show a generally high, flat-topped surface that has been cut into by rivers, creating deep valleys while the interfluves remain elevated. The map's relief pattern — with high ground interrupted by river valleys — matches this landform. An undulating lowland would show gentle, low contours throughout; marshy land appears flat and waterlogged; an old river valley would be a single broad depression rather than a plateau surface fragmented by erosion.

Measuring the railway line on the map using a string or dividers and converting with the map scale gives approximately 11.5 km. This question tests the skill of linear measurement along a curved route, not a straight-line distance. The other options — 9.5 km, 10.5 km, and 12.5 km — result from either under-measuring by not following every bend in the railway or over-measuring due to scale conversion errors.

Abag and Lobodo are most likely mining settlements because the map shows mining symbols such as mine shafts or quarry marks near them, which indicate extraction of mineral resources. Mining settlements typically grow around sites of mineral deposits and are identified by these characteristic map symbols. Educational settlements would show school symbols, commercial settlements appear near markets or road junctions with dense activity, and industrial settlements display factory or processing plant symbols — none of which match the map evidence for these two locations.

When contour lines are packed very closely together on a topographic map, they indicate a steep slope because the land rises or falls sharply over a short horizontal distance. East of Parko-Gbo Road, the contours are densely spaced, confirming a steep gradient. A gentle slope would show widely spaced contours, while a convex slope curves outward like the top of a hill and a concave slope curves inward like a bowl — neither of which matches the pattern here. Always count and compare spacing of contours to determine slope steepness.

The northern part of the map shows dense forest vegetation indicated by the forest symbols or green shading, making lumbering (the cutting and processing of timber) the most logical human activity there. Fishing requires a significant water body nearby, mining needs mineral deposits usually marked on the map, and quarrying involves extracting stone from rocky outcrops — none of these features dominate the northern section. Dense natural forest cover strongly points to timber exploitation as the primary economic activity.

To find the river's length, you trace its course on the map using a piece of string or dividers to account for all its bends and meanders, then measure the total length and convert using the map scale. River Tere winds considerably from the map edge to its confluence with River Epe, so shorter estimates like 3.70km or 4.70km undercount its meandering course. The correct measurement converts to approximately 6.70km when the map scale is properly applied. Always follow the river's actual curved path, not a straight-line distance.

A bearing is measured clockwise from True North (000°), so you draw a north line at Kosi, then measure the angle clockwise to the direction of Olefi. A bearing of 305° places Olefi in the northwest direction from Kosi, which matches the relative positions of those two settlements on the map. Options like 035° (northeast), 085° (nearly east), and 127° (southeast) all point in completely different directions. Always start your protractor measurement from north and go clockwise to avoid errors.

Two places are intervisible if a straight line drawn between them on a cross-section profile does not dip below the intervening ground surface. Kera and Kosi have a ridge or high ground lying between them that blocks the line of sight, making them not intervisible. The other pairs — Epe and Karaga, Oziza and Pheku, Tere and Olefi — do not have significant high ground interrupting the profile between them, so observers at one location can see the other. Drawing a cross-section and checking whether terrain intersects the line of sight is the standard method to test intervisibility.

Proportional circles, also called graduated circles, are map symbols whose size directly represents the magnitude of a value — population figures vary so widely between places that circles scaled to match these numbers communicate the differences clearly at a glance. Options B and C are wrong because transport and traffic data are better shown using flow lines or desire lines, where the width or thickness of the line carries the quantity. Rainfall data in D is displayed using isohyets, which are lines connecting places of equal rainfall, not circles.

On topographic and sketch maps, settlement size is judged by the area covered by the settlement symbol or the density of buildings shown. Kosi appears as the second largest settlement based on its extent on the map. Oziza, Tere, and Pkeku are represented as smaller settlements, with only the largest settlement surpassing Kosi in size. Map reading questions like this require careful comparison of settlement symbols, not just name recognition.

To find the length of a winding river on a map, you use a piece of thread or a strip of paper to follow every curve of the river, then measure that length against the map scale. Applying this method from the boundary at Ijer to the confluence with River Ayila gives approximately 5.7 km. Options A and B overestimate the distance, while D underestimates it significantly, likely from measuring a straight-line distance rather than following the river's actual course.

Sabe town's growth and position are explained by the presence of mineral resources, which attract workers and industry, and transportation routes, which allow minerals and goods to be moved in and out efficiently — mining settlements almost always develop alongside good transport links. Option B is incorrect because rivers alone rarely determine a town's location unless they serve as trade routes. Option C, latitude, is far too broad a factor to explain a specific town's siting. Option A combines agriculture with minerals, but agriculture is not mentioned as a key feature of Sabe's location on the map.

The south west of the map receives adequate rainfall and has low-lying, sometimes waterlogged terrain, conditions that favour rice cultivation, and warm humid temperatures that suit sugarcane. Cocoa in options A and B requires a specific forest zone with well-drained soils and a dry season — it thrives in Nigeria's south west forest belt but is not a match for the conditions indicated in this map's south west region. Coffee in option D needs cooler highland conditions, making it unsuitable for a low-lying, humid south west area.

Road transport earns all three described merits because roads are cheaper to construct and maintain than railway tracks, airports, or seaports, making maintenance costs relatively low. Unlike rail (fixed tracks), air (requires airports), or water (needs navigable routes), road transport can reach virtually any location — villages, farms, urban centres — giving it unmatched flexibility and network coverage. Rail transport is inflexible because trains must follow fixed routes, air transport serves only major terminals, and water transport is geographically limited to coasts, rivers, and lakes, each disqualifying them from this description.

Cotton is Mali's dominant export crop and a major source of foreign exchange earnings; the country is among sub-Saharan Africa's largest cotton producers. Groundnuts are predominantly associated with Senegal and parts of northern Nigeria, not Mali. Cocoa requires the humid, high-rainfall conditions of coastal West African countries like Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire, whereas Mali's Sahel climate is too dry for cocoa cultivation. Cattle exist in Mali but contribute far less to export revenue than cotton.

It is important to note a discrepancy here: the feature described — magma intruding horizontally along bedding planes of sedimentary rocks — is the geological definition of a sill (option A), not a dyke. A dyke (option C) is a sheet intrusion that cuts across existing rock layers, typically at a steep or vertical angle. A laccolith is a dome-shaped intrusion that arches overlying strata upward, and a batholith is a massive, deep-seated igneous body. Students should cross-check this question against their textbooks, as the description best matches a sill.

To find the population of ward 4, read its percentage share from the chart and apply it to the total population of 500,000. Ward 4 represents 15% of the city's population, so the calculation is 15/100 × 500,000 = 75,000. The other options correspond to different percentage shares — 100,000 would be 20%, 125,000 would be 25%, and 150,000 would be 30% — none of which match ward 4's segment on the chart.

Map area is calculated by measuring the length and width of the mapped area using the map's scale, then multiplying them together. Using the given scale and the grid dimensions shown on the map, the ground distance works out to approximately 10 km by 10 km, giving an area of 100 km². Options like 125 km² and 115 km² overestimate the dimensions, while 95 km² underestimates them; only 100 km² matches the actual measurements derived from the map's scale.

Bearing is measured clockwise from north (0°), so a bearing of 21° places Jata in a north-northeast direction from Adaba. On the map, the angle from the north line at Adaba toward Jata measures approximately 21°. Options A (29°) and D (25°) are close but represent slightly wider eastward angles that do not match the plotted direction. Option B (170°) is completely wrong — that would place Jata almost due south of Adaba.

A choropleth map uses different shading or colour intensities to represent statistical data across defined areas, making it an ideal alternative to a chart that shows proportional or percentage data by region. The divided rectangle is essentially a bar/band chart and shows the same data in a similar linear format rather than offering a true alternative. A dot map shows distribution by point density, not proportional values. Proportional circles represent total quantities by circle size, which suits absolute values rather than the relative data typically shown in the original chart.

A flood plain is a flat, low-lying area beside a river that forms when the river deposits sediment as it overflows its banks repeatedly over time, and contour lines on the map would be widely spaced at the centre indicating flat terrain. An erosional plain is carved by running water removing material, which produces a different landform pattern. An outwash plain is formed by glacial meltwater depositing material beyond an ice sheet, uncommon in Nigerian geography. A deltaic plain forms specifically at the mouth of a river where it enters the sea or lake, not inland at the centre of a river valley map.

Flood-liable areas in Northern Nigeria (called fadamas) are waterlogged or seasonally inundated, making sugar-cane, rice, and bananas the best combination because all three crops are tolerant of or even thrive in high-moisture, flooded conditions. Rice is a classic wetland crop planted in standing water, sugar-cane needs abundant water to grow tall, and bananas do well in moist, well-watered lowlands. Cassava is an upland crop that roots rot easily in waterlogged soil, which eliminates options A, B, and C. Yam also requires well-drained soil, making option B unsuitable for flood-prone zones.

Major mountain belts like the Alps, Himalayas, Andes, and Rockies were created by tectonic folding — when two crustal plates collide, the rock layers between them are compressed, buckle, and fold upward to form large mountain ranges. Weathering is a destructive process that breaks rocks down into smaller particles; it cannot build mountains. Wind erosion removes and transports material, further reducing landforms rather than raising them. River deposition builds up sediment in valleys and plains, not tall mountain belts.

OPEC stands for Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries, and petroleum (mineral oil) is the commodity it controls and regulates among member nations. Member countries like Nigeria, Saudi Arabia, and Venezuela all share petroleum as their major export. Coffee is associated with organisations like the ICO, while iron and steel relate to manufacturing industries, not OPEC. Vegetable oil is an agricultural product with no connection to this organisation.

Christmas Day falls on 25th December, which is during the Southern Hemisphere's summer because the Earth is tilted with the South Pole facing the sun. This means places in the Southern Hemisphere experience their longest days around that period. At 45°S, the sun is high in the sky for the longest duration among the options given. Locations in the Northern Hemisphere like 45°N and 30°N experience their shortest days in December, not the longest. The equator at 0° has roughly equal day and night throughout the year.

Annual temperature range is calculated by subtracting the lowest monthly temperature from the highest monthly temperature. The highest temperature is 19°C in July, and the lowest is -11°C in January, giving a range of 19 minus (-11) which equals 30°C. Many students mistakenly add only the positive values or forget to account for the negative temperature correctly. Option A (20°C) and D (10°C) result from arithmetic errors, while C (40°C) greatly overestimates the difference.

The station shows cold winters reaching -11°C and warm summers reaching 19°C, with precipitation spread across all months, which are classic features of a cool temperate continental climate. A warm temperate climate would have much milder winters, rarely falling below 0°C. Mediterranean climate is characterised by dry hot summers and wet winters, which does not match this data since summer here has high rainfall. Cold temperate climates would show even more extreme freezing conditions for most of the year, often below -20°C in winter.

Steel production requires large deposits of iron ore and coal, and Cuba is a small island nation with very limited reserves of both essential raw materials. India, Germany, and Japan are all significant steel producers, though Japan imports most of its raw materials and compensates with advanced technology and industry. Cuba lacks both the natural resources and the heavy industrial base needed for large-scale steel manufacturing. Among the options, no other country matches Cuba's limited potential for this industry.

Petroleum forms from the remains of tiny marine organisms that died and settled in layers on ancient sea floors over millions of years. These layers were buried and compressed into sedimentary rocks, where heat and pressure converted the organic matter into oil and gas. Sedimentary rocks like sandstone and limestone have the porous structure that traps petroleum in reservoirs. Igneous, volcanic, and plutonic rocks form from molten magma at very high temperatures that would destroy any organic material. Metamorphic rocks are transformed by extreme heat and pressure, also making petroleum survival impossible in them.

Limestone is the single mineral that connects all four locations: Ewekoro in Ogun State, Nkalagu in Enugu State, Calabar in Cross River State, and Sokoto State all have significant limestone deposits that support cement production across Nigeria. The Ewekoro and Nkalagu deposits are particularly famous as the foundation of major cement factories in Nigeria. Coal is associated mainly with the Enugu-Okaba belt, not all four locations. Gypsum is strongly associated with Sokoto alone, while iron ore is found in Itakpe and Lokoja areas, not these four zones.

To find the scale, convert both measurements to the same unit: 4 km equals 400,000 cm, while the map distance is 2 cm. Dividing: 2 divided by 400,000 gives 1 divided by 200,000, which is written as 1:200,000. Option A (1:100,000) would mean 2 cm represents only 2 km on the ground, which is too small. Option C (1:50,000) would mean 2 cm represents just 1 km, far too small. Always convert land distance to centimetres before calculating scale.

Shifting cultivation is the most ancient farming method, practised long before any other system, in which farmers clear forest land using fire, farm the same plot for two or three seasons, then permanently abandon it and move to clear fresh forest elsewhere. It is considered more primitive than bush fallowing because in bush fallowing the farmer returns to the same land after a rest period, making it a later improvement. Mixed farming, which combines crop growing with animal rearing, is a more organised and advanced system. Market gardening is a modern, intensive, commercial practice found near urban centres and is among the most recent agricultural systems.

Orogeny is the large-scale tectonic process where two crustal plates collide, forcing rock strata to buckle, bend, and fold upward into massive mountain ranges over millions of years. Fold mountains like the Himalayas, Alps, and Andes are the direct products of this plate collision and folding process. Block mountains form through faulting, where sections of crust are uplifted or dropped along fault lines, not by folding. Volcanic mountains result from magma erupting through the crust, while residual mountains are simply ancient highlands left standing after surrounding rock was worn away by erosion.

East Africa's Great Rift Valley system makes Kenya and Tanzania home to Africa's greatest volcanic regions, featuring giants like Mount Kilimanjaro, Mount Kenya, and the Virunga chain — all products of intense tectonic activity along the rift. The Maghrib's mountains (Atlas Range) are fold mountains formed by plate collision, not volcanism. Mount Cameroon exists and is active, but it is a single isolated volcano, not a major volcanic region. Sudan and Ethiopia have some volcanic features, but they cannot match the scale and concentration found along the East African Rift.

Poor transport systems directly prevent food from reaching people who need it — food may exist in surplus regions but cannot be moved to deficit areas without roads, railways, and functioning infrastructure. The question targets access specifically, not production, which rules out answers about education or natural resource development that affect how much food is grown. Economic inequality affects purchasing power but poor transport is the most immediate physical barrier to access. Even wealthy communities can face food shortages if roads are cut off by floods or disrepair.

Wind is unique because it functions as both an element of weather (wind speed and direction are directly measured and recorded in daily weather observations) and a control of climate (prevailing winds determine which air masses, temperatures, and moisture patterns dominate a region). Temperature is mainly an element, though it influences other variables. Rainfall is purely an element — it is what we measure, not what controls the system. Air mass acts as a control but is not itself recorded as an element the way wind, temperature, and rainfall are.

Cairo, the capital of Egypt, is Africa's largest and most densely populated city with over 20 million people packed into its metropolitan area, satisfying both conditions in the question. Abuja is Nigeria's capital but was purpose-built as a planned city and remains far less populated than Cairo. Dakar is Senegal's capital but is significantly smaller in both area and population. Cape Town, while populous, is not South Africa's capital — Pretoria (Tshwane) is the executive capital — so it fails the second condition entirely.

The Horn of Africa's coastline runs roughly parallel to the dominant moisture-bearing winds rather than facing them directly, so onshore winds skim along the coast without penetrating inland to deposit rainfall — the shape and orientation of the shoreline is therefore the key factor. Cold ocean currents do cause coastal aridity in western Africa (e.g., the Namib via the Benguela Current), but no significant cold current dominates the Horn's Indian Ocean coast in the same way. The East African highlands create a rain shadow on their leeward sides, but the Horn's dryness is primarily a coastal wind-angle phenomenon, not a highland barrier effect. Distance from tropical cyclone belts is a minor and indirect factor compared to the coastline's orientation relative to prevailing winds.

Bush burning is the primary disturbance to climax vegetation in Nigeria's Savannah belt because it destroys existing plant communities before they can reach their natural mature state, and it recurs seasonally, preventing ecological succession from completing. Farmers and herders burn large areas annually to clear land and stimulate new grass growth, which repeatedly resets vegetation to early successional stages. Animal grazing also degrades vegetation but is less destructive than fire across vast areas. Lumbering and mining affect isolated zones, not the broad savannah belt.

Transportation is Nigeria's most capital-intensive sector today because it requires massive investment in infrastructure such as roads, railways, airports, seaports, and vehicles, all of which demand enormous financial outlay to build and maintain. The scale of physical infrastructure needed to connect Nigeria's vast territory makes it uniquely expensive compared to other sectors. Agriculture, though widespread, relies heavily on smallholder farming with low capital input. Mining and trading involve significant capital but do not match the infrastructural demands of transportation.

Zambia is Africa's leading copper producer, holding one of the world's largest copper reserves concentrated in the Copperbelt region, making copper the backbone of its economy and major export earner. Ghana is better known for gold production, not copper. Egypt's mineral economy centers on petroleum and phosphates. Republic of Benin has no significant copper mining industry and is not associated with major mineral exports.

The Jos Plateau and Mambilla Plateau are Nigeria's highest elevated regions, with altitudes that create cooler temperatures similar to temperate climates, making them suitable for growing crops like Irish potatoes, wheat, and strawberries that cannot thrive in Nigeria's tropical lowlands. The higher altitude reduces temperatures significantly, mimicking temperate conditions. Oban Hills and Yoruba Highlands lie at lower elevations and experience typical tropical conditions. Mandara Mountains and Biu Plateau do have some elevation, but the Jos and Mambilla Plateaus are the classical examples taught for temperate crop cultivation in Nigeria.

The prairies of North America are temperate grasslands, located in the interior of the continent where moderate rainfall and seasonal temperature variations support vast stretches of grass without sufficient moisture for tree growth. They are called temperate because they lie in the mid-latitude temperate zone, experiencing cold winters and warm summers. Tropical grasslands and savannah are found in low-latitude regions like Africa and South America. Montane grasslands occur at high altitudes on mountain slopes, which does not describe the flat, inland North American plains.

A prismatic compass measures magnetic bearings, which are the horizontal angles that features or survey lines make relative to magnetic north. This makes it the standard instrument for obtaining the direction or bearing of landmarks and survey lines in the field. It cannot measure heights, which requires a levelling instrument or theodolite. Horizontal distances are measured with chains, tapes, or electronic distance measurers, while inclination of slopes is measured with a clinometer or Abney level.

Kano has been a major urban and population centre for centuries because of its early importance as a hub of trans-Saharan trade and Islamic scholarship, both of which attracted large numbers of settlers, merchants, and migrants long before modern Nigeria existed. These twin forces of religious prestige and commercial activity created self-sustaining population growth over hundreds of years.
